#90121. What Should You Do With Pumpkins After Halloween?

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1019 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Familyhandyman ↗ Open Full Page

What Should You Do With Pumpkins After Halloween?

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1019 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Should you compost pumpkins after Halloween, toss them in the trash or leave them out for wildlife?
  • Before they migrated to North America, the Irish and Scottish immigrants who established the tradition of jack-o’-lanterns, carved turnips.
  • “One billion (with a B!),” exclaims composter Lauren Click, and that’s not good, because not everyone responsibly disposes of their jack-o’-lanterns responsibly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Should you compost pumpkins after Halloween, toss them in the trash or leave them out for wildlife? Experts explain the options.

Before they migrated to North America, the Irish and Scottish immigrants who established the tradition of jack-o’-lanterns, carved turnips. In the Newly introduced World, they started carving pumpkins, which were readily available and far more dramatic. Since then, the Halloween tradition they established in the 19th century has only grown more popular and sees more and more pumpkins discarded every year.

Sources indicate that how many? “One billion (with a B!),” exclaims composter Lauren Click, and that’s not good, because not everyone responsibly disposes of their jack-o’-lanterns responsibly.

It has been revealed that if you care about soil, wildlife and the environment in general, there really is a right way and a wrong way to dispose of pumpkins after Halloween. A gardening expert, a composting expert and a worm farmer explain the difference.

It has been revealed that definitely, yes. “There are many ways to compost a pumpkin,” claims Click. “I chop mine up into smaller pieces and feed it to my indoor worm compost farm. You can compost all parts of a pumpkin as long as it is not treated with chemicals, has no paint (so, no painted pumpkins), no glitter, and no plastic/wax/metal candle residue. You can even compost moldy/gross pumpkins!”.

It has been revealed that it’s vital to chop up the pumpkin and not throw it on the compost pile whole, adds UK gardener David Denyer. “Pumpkins decompose slowly if left whole because of their thick rind and high water content. Because of this, adding them straight to your compost can throw off the balance, making the heap turn slimy or even anaerobic, which stops it from breaking down properly.”.

One option is to give them to animal rescues and local farmers to use as feed for pigs, chickens and livestock. Click loves this option because, as she notes, many farmers compost manure, which makes it a win-win situation. The pumpkin winds up providing nourishment in the soil for more pumpkins.

Sources indicate that if you live in the city, worm farmer Scott Kent has another suggestion: “Take your leftover pumpkins is to a worm farm! Composting worms, like red wigglers, consume organic waste and create worm castings from it. Pumpkins, and most all other cucurbits for that matter, are among composting worms’ most favorite foods.”.

In a recent development, for a quick way to recycle pumpkins after Halloween that you can do at home, cut the pumpkin into small chunks and bury them in your garden. “This works like a green manure,” claims Denyer, “adding organic matter below the surface where it can decompose safely without attracting any pests or spreading disease.”.

Industry observers note that this is generally a bad idea, say our experts. Click worries about attracting wildlife to areas in which they can be harmed, but beyond that, decomposing pumpkins are not the best source of nutrition. “The acidity and mold that develops as they rot can make hedgehogs, insects, and birds unwell,” notes Denyer, who lives where hedgehogs are a thing.

In a recent development, the danger to wildlife increases if the pumpkin contains toxic materials. If you wouldn’t feed, paint, glitter or candle wax to a pet, you shouldn’t feed it to wildlife.

It has been revealed that before carving a pumpkin, most people remove the seeds. Don’t throw them out. When you roast them, they make a delicious snack. After the seeds are gone, the rind makes a good (if temporary) planter for displaying your fall blooms on the porch. Just remember to line the inside to prevent dirt from spilling out from the face you carved.

It has been revealed that composting may be the best way to recycle a pumpkin rind, but if you’re okay with a less dramatic jack-o’-lantern, a smaller pumpkin like a Hokkaido or Baby-Bear can serve a double purpose. Unlike large carving pumpkins with thick, waxy skins, these smaller varieties have thin skins and a high sugar content that make them delicious in soup.

Don’t just toss  them in the garden, warns Denyer: “Pumpkins are high in water and sugars, which means they promptly break down into a thick, slimy layer that blocks air circulation and traps moisture around plant roots. This can then encourage fungal problems, like grey mold or powdery mildew, which can spread to nearby plants.”.

It has been revealed that it’s key to check with the local waste management rules, because some communities don’t allow pumpkins in yard waste bins. If your community allows them, remove candle wax and other inorganic materials.

In a recent development, painted pumpkins present a problem: They are organic, but because of the paint, you shouldn’t throw them in organic waste, and some communities prohibit organic materials in the general trash. In such cases, cutting up and burying your pumpkins after Halloween is probably the best solution.

Recent findings suggest that if you leave a whole pumpkin out in the field, it will start decomposing about eight or 12 weeks after it’s fully ripe. Once you cut a pumpkin into smaller pieces and throw them in a compost pile, the pieces will start to rot in five to 10 days.

Sources indicate that full decomposition depends on the moisture content of the air and soil, and on the temperature. It occurs faster when there’s lots of moisture and the air is warm.

Generally, no. Most paints contain toxic chemicals that can poison the compost and the soil on which you spread it. This isn’t necessarily true for all paints, including some water-soluble plant- or egg-based children’s paints, but if you don’t know where the paint came from, keep the painted pumpkin out of the compost.

It has been revealed that A paint may be safe for kids, but that doesn’t mean it’s safe for composting. Crayola, a manufacturer of safe-to-use paints for children, recommends using them on pumpkins but warns that those pumpkins should not be consumed (meaning they should not go in the compost).

#90120. Tech Report: Yard Eyesores That Ruin Your Curb Appeal

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1067 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Familyhandyman ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Yard Eyesores That Ruin Your Curb Appeal

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1067 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Realtors weigh in on these common yard eyesores that can hurt curb appeal and make a home look less than its best.
  • Like personal style and hygiene, everyone has different rules when it comes to yard upkeep and design.
  • The good news is that nobody has to agree on what makes one yard beautiful and another an eyesore (unless you live in an HOA!), but some yard features are bound to cause a head shake or two from the neighbors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Realtors weigh in on these common yard eyesores that can hurt curb appeal and make a home look less than its best.

What makes a yard an eyesore? It depends on who you ask. Like personal style and hygiene, everyone has different rules when it comes to yard upkeep and design. One person’s cherished garden gnomes might be another’s idea of tacky kitsch. Lawn decor might be a matter of taste, but neglected maintenance like a broken fence or rotting RV in the yard are harder to overlook.

The good news is that nobody has to agree on what makes one yard beautiful and another an eyesore (unless you live in an HOA!), but some yard features are bound to cause a head shake or two from the neighbors. Ahead, find some of the most controversial yard eyesores, with a reminder that curb appeal is always subjective.

It has been revealed that unmowed grass and overgrown weeds make a yard look neglected and can swiftly crossover into eyesore territory. But that doesn’t mean everyone’s yard has to look perfectly manicured or exactly the same, either. “A yard that is basic is not a problem as long as it is well kept,” real estate broker Erik Leland states. “You could choose a meadow-style yard or a pollinator garden as long as it is intentional with defined paths and maintained edges.”.

Vibrant, healthy trees and shrubs add to a home’s curb appeal, but neglected, overgrown or dead ones can promptly tank it. Even if the rest of the yard is well-maintained, lifeless hedges and trees make it look like an eyesore. “Dead shrubs may appear minor. However, they create a larger perception problem if the property owner is not maintaining something minor, like dead shrubs,” real estate agent Ben Mizes notes.

Broken or unused bulky items like patio furniture, piles of lumber, old furniture or broken lawn equipment can swiftly pile up in the yard and become an eyesore. Difficult to dispose of, these items can overwhelm homeowners. “When you see clutter and junk in or around a home, it can create stress and uneasiness, even for neighbors,” Realtor Dell Jeanty claims. “Keeping the yard organized can make the property and the entire street feel cleaner and more welcoming.”.

Industry observers note that fences can add to a home’s curb appeal and value, but a neglected one is just a yard eyesore. Broken, rotting and leaning fences drag down a property’s appeal and give the impression it’s not cared for. However, “a fence does not have to be fresh to look good,” real estate expert Cameron Walker notes. “Old fences can be painted, and neglected and damaged fences can be repaired to make a good first impression.”.

Recent findings suggest that adding statues and garden gnomes to your yard is a personal choice that not everyone will enjoy. What makes you smile may make your neighbor scratch their head. But, even if you are a fan, it is possible to have too much of a good thing. “The right amount of decorations can give personality to a yard and make it inviting, but too many can give a cluttered appearance,” Walker states. “Decorations should be placed to give ample space to display the landscaping.”.

While low-maintenance artificial turf is appealing, it can look like an eyesore if not done correctly. Low-quality material and shoddy installation methods result in uneven seams and a cheap aesthetic. “One of the major problems is if it appears as if the grass has been glued to the ground,” Mizes notes. But, even when done right, some people just don’t like the look of fake turf. It comes down to personal preference.

According to recent reports, A few carefully placed ornaments can give a yard character, but too many create an eyesore of visual clutter. “A property can lose appeal with an overabundance of various garden ornaments competing for focal points throughout the landscape,” Mizes says. “[But] a collection within a defined area of the landscape can be better appreciated.” Just know that your vision of a beautiful yard might look like a flea market to your neighbor.

“There’s nothing wrong with having garbage and recycling bins in the front yard during pick-up day, but leaving them lined up in front of the house all week doesn’t look great and robs the home of its curb appeal,” Jeanty claims. “Tucking them beside the house or behind a small screen keeps the yard looking cleaner.” On the other hand, some folks just don’t see what the major deal is about hiding trash cans and that’s okay, too.

Broken down cars, ATVs or campers strewn in a yard qualify as a yard eyesore in most people’s eyes. Mice settle in, lawn and weeds grow around it and your property can start to resemble a junk yard. It knocks down your curb appeal and impacts your home’s value and your neighbor’s, too. A non-working vehicle doesn’t automatically constitute an eyesore, though, if it’s stored intentionally and preferably out of sight.

While they may spread holiday cheer, not everyone cares for inflatable yard decorations. Where some see whimsy, others see tacky. No matter which side you’re on, most would agree that when deflated during the day, inflatables turn into a yard eyesore. “They just look like piles of plastic in your yard,” Leland says. Additionally, too many inflatables can be fun or make a yard look disorganized and cluttered, depending on your take.

“A derelict shed or rotting play structure is sure to give a bad impression,” Leland claims. “If it’s not worth repairing, remove it. An empty space is the better choice.” When I moved into my current home, one of the first things we did was remove a large gazebo that was long past its prime. Our latest neighbors all came by and thanked us for removing the neighborhood eyesore.

Sources indicate that kitschy lawn ornaments like plastic flamingos could elicit an eye roll from a neighbor, but perhaps not. “A couple of plastic flamingos can be funny and add personality to a yard, so I wouldn’t automatically call them an eyesore,” Jeanty notes. “But when there are twenty of them with mismatched colors competing with signs, flags and other decorations, it becomes a little overwhelming.” Thoughtfully incorporate your outdoor decor into the landscape for a more tasteful display.

#90119. John Yoo on "Leaving a [University of] California that Rejects the West"

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (541 w)
📖 Baca

John Yoo on "Leaving a [University of] California that Rejects the West"

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (541 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that professor John Yoo is leaving the law school at the University of California at Berkeley to join the School of Civic Leadership at the University of Texas at Austin.
  • Given the attention his move has received, Yoo has written an op-ed for the Latest York Post explaining his decision to choose Texas, and disputing any suggestion that he was driven out of Berkeley.
  • I'm leaving not because I feel driven out by Berkeley — anything but.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that professor John Yoo is leaving the law school at the University of California at Berkeley to join the School of Civic Leadership at the University of Texas at Austin. As I noted here, his departure means there will not be a single right-leaning professor teaching public law subjects at Berkeley--and no more than a handful (if that) at all of the UC schools combined.

Given the attention his move has received, Yoo has written an op-ed for the Latest York Post explaining his decision to choose Texas, and disputing any suggestion that he was driven out of Berkeley.

I'm leaving not because I feel driven out by Berkeley — anything but.

In my three decades there I've enjoyed working, on an individual level, with spirited, ambitious students and challenging, innovative scholars.

I'm moving because Berkeley, like its peers, has declined from a daring, risk-taking center of higher learning to one that wallows contentedly in a monoculture of liberalism.

Yoo indicates the school has been obsessed with ethnic diversity while disregarding viewpoint diversity, and that this has eroded the institution's commitment to free speech and created an environment in which anti-semitism has taken root.

I've watched students and the usual agitators disrupt debates on affirmative action, spark pitched fights on Sproul Plaza and try to shout down distinguished scholars and thinkers (home of the Free Speech Movement, indeed).

Tolerance of such shenanigans was matched by intolerance of conservative or libertarian views on the faculty.

According to recent reports, berkeley has consistently rejected conservative scholars, no matter how well-qualified, well-published or widely cited. . . .

Sources indicate that one famous member of a revered Berkeley humanities department (always ranked among the nation's top three) once told me directly that he would never hire a conservative. . . .

Most student groups at Berkeley Law now boycott any event with a speaker who believes in Israel's right to exist.

For the first time in my 33 years at Berkeley I witnessed a heckler's veto, as protesters prevented a member of the Israeli Knesset from speaking — and top university officials stood idly by.

Students posted flyers depicting the dean of the law school — a liberal scholar with whom I rarely agree — feasting on human beings, then physically invaded his home while he hosted members of the graduating class, simply because he is Jewish.

Yoo argues that great universities should refocus their teaching on Western Civilization, so that the nation does not lose sight of the ideals upon which it was founded and the principles that provide the foundation for western prosperity.

The emergence of human reason in Greece and religious revelation in Jerusalem produced the free markets, natural rights, rule of law and democratic self-government that have made our astounding prosperity and power possible.

In a recent development, everyone recognizes an emergency siren. Or do they?

Industry observers note that officers can choose different tones to make their vehicles easier to notice on busy streets or open roads. Some departments also use certain sounds for special warnings. With electronic siren systems offering several options, drivers might hear multiple tones during a single emergency response.

Learn what the common sounds mean, why officers switch between them, whether different tones signal different emergencies, and how drivers should react.

Different police siren sounds serve different purposes, but they don’t necessarily indicate specific emergencies. Officers often switch tones based on traffic conditions or to get drivers’ attention. A faster siren doesn’t always mean a more serious emergency.

The most common police siren sounds include:.

It has been revealed that modern police vehicles typically use electronic sirens that allow officers to switch between these sounds. Older mechanical sirens use a spinning mechanism to produce a traditional wail.

Officers also adjust their sirens based on traffic conditions. Faster tones can help get drivers’ attention in heavy traffic, while a slower wail may work on quieter roads. Departments set their own policies for siren use, so there isn’t one standard sound for daytime or nighttime driving.

Regardless of the siren sound, drivers should respond the same way when an emergency vehicle approaches. Drivers should check their mirrors, signal, and safely pull toward the right side of the road to let the police vehicle pass. They should avoid sudden braking or stopping in an intersection.

Anyone already in an intersection should continue through before pulling over. Drivers waiting at a red light shouldn’t enter the intersection unless an officer directs them to do so. After the police vehicle passes, drivers should check for other emergency vehicles before returning to traffic. Specific rules may vary by state.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Salt your driveway like a pro this winter with these expert-backed tips.

The Centers for Disease Control report a 35 percent increase in outdoor slips and falls during the winter months. Icy sidewalks, stairs and driveways are largely to blame for this seasonal uptick. Icy driveways are not only dangerous to walk on but also make driving and parking difficult. Ice melt salt is one of the best ways to keep driveways clear, but how should you best use it? Should you apply it before or after a storm — or both? Two industry experts weigh in on the best way to salt your driveway for optimal results this winter.

In a recent development, it depends. Salting before a massive storm with heavy snow and ice accumulation is a good idea, but timing matters.

Industry observers note that initiative to apply salt several hours before a storm hits for best results. It creates a salty coating that prevents the initial snowfall from bonding with the driveway surface. Pre-salting reduces total snow accumulation and makes snow removal easier once the storm is over. Avoid doing it too far in advance, or if rain is in the forecast, as the salt can be washed or blown away before the snow arrives. It’s not necessary to salt before a light snowfall of less than six inches.

It has been revealed that it’s always a good idea to salt after it snows, but don’t rely on it to replace snow removal efforts. First remove as much snow as possible with a shovel or snowblower, then use salt to clear away any remaining slush and snow.

Recent findings suggest that the best time to salt is immediately after snow removal, before cold nighttime temperatures set in. “When applied before the temperatures drop, salt prevents ice from forming and ensures the snow does not freeze solid to the ground,” Angelika Klimorowski, a winter maintenance specialist at Online Rock Salt, notes.

Apply salt before and after a massive storm for best results, especially when heavy snow, sleet or freezing rain is expected.

“Pre-salting helps prevent ice from bonding to the driveway, while a second application can help break down any ice that forms,” Aaron Strickland, owner of Mr. Trim Lawn & Garden Services, claims. “For a typical snowfall, both applications usually aren’t necessary.”.

According to recent reports, if only a few inches of snow is forecast, salting after snow removal is likely sufficient. Applying salt before and after a small storm is not only a waste of money, but can damage driveway surfaces, burn lawn edges and generate harmful storm runoff.

“The exact amount of rock salt that you need will depend on how substantial the area is that you are planning to de-ice,” Klimorowski notes. A little goes a long way, and more is not better. A 12-oz. coffee mug filled with salt is enough to treat a 1,000-sq.-ft. driveway. Spread salt evenly, leaving about 3 inches between salt grains. Avoid overapplication, as it can degrade driveway surfaces and harm the environment.

Industry observers note that A handheld spreader makes application easier and more consistent, especially for larger driveways. “We try to follow recommended coverage rates and use a spreader wherever possible,” Strickland indicates. “Too much salt wastes product and can damage surrounding grass and gardens.” If spreading salt by hand, always wear gloves and cascade it for even coverage.

Rock salt is only effective down to ground temperatures of 15 to 17 degrees. Don’t apply more salt if it’s not working, as it’s likely too cold out for it to work. “If your area tends to experience colder temperatures, you may need to find an alternative de-icing product to keep your surfaces safe,” Klimorowski says. Calcium chloride and magnesium chloride ice melt products are two common alternatives that remain effective at sub-zero temperatures.

Industry observers note that yes, rain will wash away salt rather than dissolve it. It then ends up in storm drains and potentially pollutes local bodies of water.

Rock salt stops working in temperatures below 10 to 15 degrees.

“While it is true that salt will work best if you apply it before the temperatures drop, there is no deadline, and you can always apply it later,” Klimorowski notes.

There’s no guarantee salt will damage your driveway, but you should use it sparingly. Concrete driveways are particularly vulnerable to salt damage.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

From lawns to sealed concrete, you might be surprised at how much damage a snow shovel can do.

It has been revealed that clearing snow from walkways is vital for safety, but winter shoveling can easily damage wooden decks, asphalt driveways and other surfaces. So, as the days get shorter and colder, it’s important to solidify your shoveling strategy before the first snow flies.

“Snow can camouflage uneven areas and patches of ice, posing slip-and-fall risks, particularly when you’re rushing to shovel,” says landscaping expert Jose Lopez. “Being mindful and taking a relaxed, careful approach will help you save money and keep everyone safe all winter long.”.

Ahead, experts walk through how to shovel eleven tricky surfaces around your home, to keep everyone safe, plus prevent costly springtime repairs.

According to recent reports, shoveling gravel is frustrating because those pebbles tend to come up with the snow, then get scattered onto the landscaping. “You will end up cleaning about $150 worth of it off your lawn in the spring,” states grading and paving contractor Scott Flores.

Sources indicate that to make life easier, use a plastic shovel, keep the blade about an inch above the gravel and clear the snow in short passes. “You don’t have to expose all of the gravel,” says Lopez. “It’s fine to leave a thin layer of snow behind.”.

Industry observers note that A metal snow shovel blade can actually scratch and gouge concrete. “It can cause $3,000 worth of damage to your pavement in 20 minutes and you won’t know it ’til April,” claims Flores. Initially, the damage “may not look like much, but once water gets under it and freezes, it will cause spalling and make your pavement look 10 years older than it is.”.

Luckily, the fix is easy on this one: always use a poly-blade (plastic) or rubber-edged shovel on concrete.

Aliaksandr Bahdanovich/Getty Images.

Aggressive shoveling can damage paint and sealers, even if they’re touted as “scratch-resistant.” “That layer is about three millimeters thick, and your steel shovel will chip it away like you’re peeling your fingernails,” says Flores.

According to recent reports, the fix: use a poly-blade shovel, shovel with a slight upward motion and leave a half-inch of snow for the sun to melt, indicates Flores. “Many believe that steel shovels will last longer. Yes they will, but that’s what makes them bad,” he says.

Pro-tip: If you use a deicer, make sure it’s safe for your particular coating, states Lopez.

It has been revealed that just like with concrete, asphalt seems indestructible, but metal shovels can damage it, especially if it already has imperfections or cracks. So, the best approach is to use a poly-blade (plastic) or rubber-edged shovel, and shovel the snow before it partially melts and refreezes.

“Avoid pushing your shovel into cracks or potholes, and don’t bang it against the surface in an attempt to dislodge stubborn ice,” says Lopez. “Instead, choose a deicing product that’s safe for asphalt.”.

Recent findings suggest that A shovel can easily catch the edge of a paver and scratch, break or knock it out of place. To prevent that, use a poly-blade shovel, take shorter shovel strokes, push snow at an angle and slightly raise up the leading edge.

“Shoveling and deicing aggressively won’t make your job faster or easier, it takes some finesse,” indicates Lopez. Also, use de-icers that are safe for both the paving and jointing material, and inspect the walkway for loose bricks once the snow melts.

It has been revealed that after a snow, it can be tricky to tell where the concrete ends and the lawn begins, and one wrong move means damaged grass come springtime. To keep from marring your grass, mark walkway edges with small flags before it snows. While shoveling, keep the blade even with your walkway, versus angling it toward the grass.

In a recent development, pro-tip: “Slow down and work in short passes near the edges, rather than trying to force the shovel along,” says Lopez. “.

Try not to pile snow on shrubs and other perennials, as that can snap branches. It’s also best to keep deicers and their runoff away from landscaping.

“Before winter arrives, plan where you’ll pile or toss snow to keep it away from sensitive plants,” notes Lopez. “You may find it helpful to use a smaller shovel, which will give you better control over where the snow lands.”.

Also, try not to move soil, which can expose plants to the cold, and never strike frozen branches to remove snow. “Wood breaks more easily than people expect,” says moving professional Leon Schwab.

Aggressive shoveling is sure to damage a deck, regardless of its composition. To preserve yours, use a poly-blade shovel and push the snow in the direction of the boards. If it’s safe to do so, leave a thin layer of snow, instead of shoveling all the way down to bare decking, then apply a deicer that’s recommended for the surface type.

In a recent development, safety tip: “If wet, heavy snow is accumulating and you notice the deck sagging or hear creaking noises, seek professional advice,” claims Lopez. “Don’t continue using the deck if you suspect a structural issue.”.

Stairs are particularly hazardous when its slippery out, and clearing them can be precarious, with snow obscuring their boundaries and confined spaces limiting your range of motion.

To stay safe, “Wear boots with good traction and make sure your staircase is well lit,” says Lopez. “Don’t rush the job. It’s better to take your time and shovel safely.”.

Pro-tip: “Use a small shovel to clear one step at a time and maintain a stable position,” claims Schwab.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes it’s prudent to clear large accumulations of snow from the roof, but it’s also a dangerous job. To stay safe, roofing contractor Andre Kazimierski recommends using a roof rake, which allows you to pull off snow while remaining on the ground. Focus on clearing off as much as you can, but don’t worry about leaving it completely bare, and try not to touch your roofing material.

In a recent development, “Do this sooner rather than later, because if it starts to warm up a bit the snow will become denser and heavier, making it harder to remove,” states Kazimierski. “And never walk on your roof when it’s even the slightest bit snowy or icy up there.”.

It has been revealed that obviously, you don’t want to take a shovel to your car, as that would do a lot of damage. Instead, use a snow brush or broom that’s designed to be gentle on vehicle finishes. Flores recommends this one from Snow Joe.

Start by clearing the roof in sections, then move on to the hood, trunk, windows, headlights, taillights and mirrors. You’ll especially want to get the roof and hood fully clear; otherwise, once you start driving, snow can blow up or slide down onto your windshield, obstructing your vision and endangering other drivers. “That ice can fly off your car at 40 miles per hour,” says Flores.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, last week, Professor Mark W. Smith released his new 85-minute film discussing the operations and mechanics of modern firearms, including semiautomatic rifles such as the popular AR-15 rifle. The film, titled "Firearms and the AR-15 Rifle: A Primer for the Bench and Bar," can be found on YouTube here and on Rumble. It has already been viewed over 23,000 times since its release only days ago. The film is broken down into 25 segments so a viewer can jump from topic to topic.

That federal judges are now reviewing Internet videos to learn about firearms is hardly surprising. A few weeks ago Judge Doris Pryor of the Seventh Circuit made reference to this during oral argument in a constitutional fight over the legality of Illinois's suppressor ban. In the consolidated cases of Anderson v. Raoul and Morse v. Raoul, argued October 28, 2026, she acknowledged that she has watched videos in preparing for oral argument. The oral argument audio recording is here with Judge Pryor's comment at the 25:04-25:23 mark.

It has been revealed that as I previously wrote, I had the pleasure of introducing the "AR-15 Primer" film. From there, Rick Vasquez (a former ATF firearm technician and U.S. Marine ordnance officer) takes the spotlight explaining the mechanical operation of today's AR-15 rifle and its typical features.

Industry observers note that but there is another notable aspect of the film that is worth noting. And that is the impressive animations found within the film that help educate legal professionals and the general public about the internal and related operations of the AR-15 (and most modern semi-automatic rifles).

According to recent reports, the animations found throughout the film are informative for those learning about firearm mechanics. Here are a few of the noteworthy ones:.

There is an excellent 2-minute animation illustrating how gas-operated semiautomatic rifles internally deploy the rapidly-expanding gases from the firing of a shot to do two things: first, to send a projectile (the bullet) down the barrel and, second, to prepare the rifle to fire the next round of ammunition. This is called autoloading. This dual use of the gases from firing a single shot is generally not understood or appreciated by those fresh to firearms technology, but the film's animation makes it clear. This animation also clarifies that autoloading does not mean automatic fire (like one sees with a M16 machine gun). The animation can be seen at the 14:58 to 17:58 mark of the film.

Industry observers note that the film also does a nice job demonstrating the physical reality of recoil by illustrating how the features of an AR-15 like the straight line stock, the buffer spring/buffer tube, and the muzzle brake help to minimize recoil allowing for a more comfortable and effective shooting experience. The 28:09 to 28:22 mark has a nice illustration of the straight-line stock while the 28:28 to 28:59 mark illustrates the role of the buffer and buffer spring in minimizing uncomfortable recoil. The 27:59 to 28:07 mark highlights an animation illustrating what constitutes recoil from the firing of a rifle.

In a recent development, the film also effectively uses animation to illustrate the difference between scopes, red dot optics, and iron sights. A scope magnifies the target making it appear closer than it really is; a red dot optic helps the user aim the rifle using an electronic dot without magnification; and iron sights entail aligning a front post with a rear sight. The 1:00:53 to 1:01:18 mark illustrates these differences.

In a recent development, animation also helps viewers understand that the barrel of a semiautomatic rifle gets hot when the rifle is fired due to the internal gas explosion that results from firing a round. The film's animation shows the rifle barrel heating up and demonstrates the value of handguards (often called "barrel shrouds" in legislation) to protect the user of the rifle. The 46:24 to 46:33 mark illustrates a barrel heating up as the rifle is shot.

The film's use of animations to explain the difference between a bullet and a cartridge is also worth mentioning. Lawyers (and even some judges) use those terms interchangeably, but they mean very different things. The 1:10:12 to 1:11:08 mark illustrates the four components (primer, gun power, case and bullet) of a modern ammunition cartridge.

It has been noted that the late President Harry Truman embraced the thought, "I am from Missouri so you have to show me." Well, Professor Smith's fresh film on firearm mechanics works hard to "show" (through animations, illustrations and images) the internal mechanics and features of AR-15 semiautomatic rifles. And I suspect the bench and the bar will be the better for it.

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

According to recent reports, A key to the city looks official, but it won't unlock any doors. Here's why cities give them out and what recipients actually receive.

Industry observers note that whether it’s in a movie or real life, everyone has seen or heard of someone receiving an oversized gold key that is a “key to the city.” The ceremony is usually accompanied with a photoshoot, a handshake, and applause. But what does the key actually do?

Sources indicate that cities across the world still hand out these awards, and the tradition goes back much further than most people realize. Learn what a key to the city represents, how the custom began, and what someone actually gets to do with it.

A key to the city is an award that cities give to people they want to honor.

“The Key to the City is presented as a symbol of civic recognition and Philadelphia’s appreciation for individuals whose achievements, service and influence have made a meaningful impact on the city and its people,” according to a release from the City of Philadelphia.

In a recent development, the key is usually decorative, with the city’s name or seal on it. Some come in a display box or with a certificate. Little Rock, Arkansas, considers its key the city’s highest ceremonial honor.

But the key won’t open City Hall or any other public building. It doesn’t give the recipient special privileges or any authority, either. In 2010, Newly introduced York City tried something different with an art project that gave people working keys to certain locations. Those weren’t the same as the city’s usual honorary keys.

In a recent development, the tradition goes back to when cities had walls and gates that closed at night. Giving someone a key meant they could come and go without asking permission.

In medieval Europe, leaders also exchanged keys during official visits or military surrenders. Handing over the keys sometimes meant giving up control of a city. Over time, the custom became a way to welcome or honor someone.

Today, cities give keys to athletes, public figures, volunteers, and local residents. Each city has its own rules for who receives one.

Philadelphia, for example, honored a resident in 2026 after he walked across the country to support career opportunities for young people. Elk Grove, California, recognizes military accomplishments and acts of heroism, while Little Rock reserves its keys for people who live outside Arkansas.

Mayors usually present the keys, although some cities involve the city council or accept nominations from residents. Recipients get a keepsake and some public recognition, but no special privileges.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Angled parking spaces aren't just a design choice.
  • Navigating a latest parking lot can be confusing and stressful.
  • Sources indicate that parking lot designers think about how vehicles enter spaces, where drivers back out, and how much room cars need between rows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Angled parking spaces aren't just a design choice. Their layout can make turning easier, control traffic, and change how a lot uses space.

Navigating a latest parking lot can be confusing and stressful. Some have one-way traffic, some have different parking rules. Even the parking spaces themselves can vary, with some lots using straight spaces and others using diagonal parking spaces. It turns out that small difference is intentional.

Sources indicate that parking lot designers think about how vehicles enter spaces, where drivers back out, and how much room cars need between rows. Learn why some parking lots use diagonal spaces, how the layout affects traffic, and what drivers should watch for.

Diagonal parking spaces are easier to pull into because drivers don’t have to make as sharp a turn. This is especially helpful in busy lots where cars are frequently coming and going. These spaces usually face one-way lanes, allowing drivers to pull in from the same direction. This helps keep traffic moving and reduces the chance of cars approaching each other head-on.

Drivers still need to follow the arrows, though. Entering from the wrong direction makes it harder to pull into a space and can put drivers in the path of cars backing out.

It has been revealed that not always. According to the Iowa Statewide Urban Design and Specifications, “One-way angled parking provides fewer spaces than perpendicular for the same length of aisle.”.

Sources indicate that the benefit is that one-way angled parking allows for narrower driving lanes, since drivers don’t need as much room to turn. Two-way angled parking is also possible, though Iowa’s guidelines say it’s generally less efficient than other layouts.

In a recent development, there’s also a downside to consider. Backing out of an angled space can be difficult when neighboring cars block the view, especially larger trucks and SUVs.

Some streets use back-in angled parking to address this problem. Drivers back into a space so they can pull forward when leaving. According to the University of Kentucky, Kentucky Transportation Center, “With the front of their vehicle facing the street, a motorist has improved sight distance when leaving a parking space.”.

In a recent development, back-in parking also lets passengers get out toward the sidewalk and keeps loading and unloading away from traffic. For regular diagonal spaces, drivers should back out slowly and watch for approaching cars and pedestrians. Backup cameras can help, but they shouldn’t replace checking the surrounding area.

A German beauty group that makes and distributes former soccer player David Beckham’s fragrance line has kicked out at the soccer icon’s lawsuit against them, asking a New York court to dismiss the case.

The Associated Press reported Tuesday that German-based Coty has argued that the New York Supreme Court lacks jurisdiction, and that Beckham’s commercial entity DB Ventures is simply using the claim to “manufacture its early exit” from their deal to sign with another company.

DB Ventures had originally filed suit in April, alleging that Beckham’s brand of luxury colognes and fragrances were being sold at gas stations and discount stores in violation of their agreement.

According to the AP, Beckham’s name is a famous global brand synonymous with luxury and elegance.

Recent findings suggest that “Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station,” the complaint said. “How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.”.

According to the AP, DB Ventures is seeking at least $41 million in damages for breach of its licensing agreement.

Coty told the AP that it strongly disputes the claims and would not comment further on ongoing litigation. Authentic Brands, DB Ventures’ parent company, declined to comment to the AP.

Beckham, a former Manchester United, Real Madrid, AC Milan, Paris Saint-Germain and LA Galaxy player who captained the English national football team and was knighted in 2025, has built a business career that includes co-owning soccer team Inter Miami.

According to the Sunday Times, he is the first billionaire sports figure in the United Kingdom, having a combined net worth of about $1.58 billion with his wife, Victoria Beckham, a former member of the Spice Girls music group.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, ice melt salt is an effective option for preventing and removing ice from sidewalks, driveways and stairs, but it isn’t suitable for every surface.
  • Sources indicate that ice melt salt chemically reacts with certain materials, accelerates freeze-thaw cycles and alters surface moisture levels to cause damage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Avoid damaging salt-sensitive outdoor surfaces with these expert-backed suggestions.

In a recent development, ice melt salt is an effective option for preventing and removing ice from sidewalks, driveways and stairs, but it isn’t suitable for every surface. Applying ice melt to certain materials can cause significant damage and should be avoided. Ahead, learn which surfaces are most vulnerable to damage from ice melt, why it happens and what safer alternatives you can use to keep outdoor areas free from ice.

Sources indicate that ice melt salt chemically reacts with certain materials, accelerates freeze-thaw cycles and alters surface moisture levels to cause damage. The type of damage will depend on the surface and how it interacts with ice melt.

Ice melt contains rock salt, calcium chloride and/or magnesium chloride to melt ice faster and at lower temperatures. While all melting salt is corrosive and can damage outdoor surfaces, ice melt products can react differently than rock salt alone.

Ice melt seeps deeply into porous cement-based materials. The calcium chloride in ice melt can react with elements of concrete or brick to form calcium oxychloride crystals. As the crystals grow, they generate extreme pressure that can cause cracks, surface spalling and crumbling.

Sources indicate that de-icing products accelerate freeze-thaw cycles in porous cement-based surfaces, causing them to break down. “It makes the freezing and thawing cycle more aggressive, which is what causes the surface to break up,” Murphy indicates.

Though less damaging than rock salt, ice melt can still contribute to deterioration. Calcium chloride and magnesium chloride attract and retain moisture, increasing the potential for freeze-thaw damage.

Conversely, ice melt draws moisture out of organic materials, causing them to dry out. Over time, this moisture loss can lead to warping, cracking, splitting and other forms of deterioration.

Ice melt accelerates metal oxidation to create rust. It can corrode rebar embedded in concrete, potentially causing cracks and structural damage, as well as rusting exposed metal stairs and railings.

It’s best to avoid applying salt to these salt-sensitive surfaces.

It has been revealed that “New concrete is the most vulnerable because it takes weeks to fully cure, so salt on the surface will cause the top few millimeters to flake off,” Murphy says. To be safe, avoid salting new concrete for the first season.

“Cracked concrete opens up for water to get inside, and salt in the water will only make that worse because it will freeze and thaw more aggressively,” Murphy indicates.

Recent findings suggest that all ice melt products will damage hard-scape surfaces due to chemical reactions and freeze-thaw cycles. “If you are using them, use them sparingly and remove them as soon as possible to decrease continuous exposure for your hardscape areas,” Zurcher claims.

In a recent development, natural stone like limestone and flagstone can react to ice melt compounds. The porous surface is vulnerable to damaging freeze-thaw cycles as well.

Harsh de-icers can damage dyed, painted or stamped concrete surfaces by breaking down color pigments.

Metal stairs and railings will rapidly rust when salt is applied to them, so it’s best to avoid it.

Ice melt draws moisture from wood, causing cracking, warping and raised fibers. It also degrades paint and stain and leaves behind chalky white salt stains.

Sand: Sand doesn’t melt ice, but does provide traction to prevent slips.

Wood ash: Instead of throwing away wood ash, use it as a salt alternative to melt ice and also provide improved traction.

Electric mats: Installed before cold weather sets in, electric melting mats warm up and prevent ice from ever forming. These can be very effective on stairs and sidewalks.

Weed torch: Weed torches are handy when you need to melt a lot of ice rapidly. Do not use one to melt ice on wood and avoid painted or stained concrete as well.

“The best way to reduce damage from these chemicals is to shovel snow as soon as possible,” Zurcher notes, so you can use less of them. Use ice melt sparingly, and only as directed. A handful is enough to treat three square yards. Instead of using ice melt alone, mix a small amount with sand to treat surfaces.

Regular sealing protects cement-based products. “Reseal every three to five years to make sure no water can get in, salty or not,” Murphy notes. Additionally, use chloride-free de-icing products, or those labelled as “concrete-safe”.

Newly poured concrete is the most vulnerable to salt damage, but all concrete surfaces will experience damage with enough prolonged exposure to salt.

According to recent reports, it depends on the extent of the damage. Major cracks and breakage mean concrete needs to be removed and repoured, Zurcher claims, while surface damage could be skim-coated, with potentially limited results.

Pet-safe products will have similar effects on hardscape areas, Zurcher states, as they still contain salt.

Jacobin senior editor Meagan Day takes to the pages of the NYT to decry woke excess, and argue that it need not be a part of democratic socialist politics. Indeed, she fears wokism will "pull the left off course.".

In a recent development, to hear many conservatives define it, I would be considered woke. I've been a member of the Democratic Socialists of America for 10 years. I believe this country needs deep criminal justice and police reform. I am galled by ICE agents ethnically profiling and brutalizing people. I not only support gay marriage but am an enthusiastic participant in one.

But wokeness is not about a basic concern for social justice. It hyperfocuses on language and identity, fights dirty from the moral high ground and mandates deference to self-appointed spokespeople for marginalized groups. It conflates disagreement with harm, and keeps careful watch for heretics.

Day's comments are not merely based upon her experience during the Great Awokening, but also as a student at Oberlin where she saw what she calls "Woke Beta." Now she fears wokeness could derail the ability of Democrats to advance socialist priorities.

It has been revealed that president Trump's re-election quieted calls to defund and diversify. But wokeness persists today. In D.S.A., which I joined on the heels of the first Bernie Sanders presidential campaign, one still encounters debates about whether clapping is ableist or whether socialists should commit to "decolonizing 'Minnesota.'" At its best, D.S.A. strikes me as our greatest shot at building a broad-based and politically serious organized left. At its worst, the energy reminds me of a scene from an Oberlin dining co-op, where a group of members filed in during a meal and silently unfurled a sign reading, "This co-op is messed up." (They were protesting the privilege inherent in cliques; the sign's wording was in fact less polite.).

Recent findings suggest that the next Congress can't let these debates trickle up again. The freshman representatives from the bluest districts, such as those in Brooklyn and Los Angeles, will still face pressure to spend their time denouncing offensive language and censuring members to their right. Instead, they should focus on making life better for working-class people — working toward Medicare for all, labor law reform, maybe even a Green Fresh Deal. For the first time in a while, the moderate members of their party might actually be open to compromising on these concerns.

As for wokeness, I suspect that many progressive elected officials are privately rankled by its excesses, but publicly inclined to ignore it, worried about inviting moral hectoring from the left. The most productive thing they can do now is grow a backbone. They need to take it upon themselves to elevate the best, most compelling ideas even when doing so earns them some pushback.

In a recent development, day's arguments, including her suggestion that DSA types should embrace "carceral minimalism" instead of prison abolition--what she calls a "nonsensical position"--is facing pushback from the Left. We will see whether the fresh Democratic majority takes her advice.

  • With autumn in full swing, it’s time to start thinking about preparing for the looming winter months.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Avoid injury with these expert-backed snow shoveling safety tips.

With autumn in full swing, it’s time to start thinking about preparing for the looming winter months. If you live in a snow-prone climate, this means getting out the shovels, salt and snowblower before the first flakes fly. Even if you’re not new to shoveling, it’s worth learning how to do it safely, as injuries can occur at any time.

Shoveling may seem simple, but can lead to strains, pulls and cardiac events if not done properly. Ahead, learn expert-backed tips to shovel snow the right (and safe) way with insights from cardiologist Dr. Bradley Serwer.

In a recent development, the safest way to shovel snow is to push it as much as possible and avoid lifting. If you must lift snow to remove it, bend at the knees and lift with your legs instead of your back.

In a recent development, “The most important tool when preparing to shovel snow is good common sense,” Serwer notes. “Dress appropriately and consider the risks of the job at hand.”.

Dress in layers that allow you to remove or open up a layer of clothing as you warm up to avoid getting overheated. Opt for a moisture wicking base layer, a mid-weight layer and a jacket that is wind-resistant and waterproof. Wear warm, waterproof gloves, a hat, warm socks and thick-soled winter boots. For particularly cold temperatures and high winds, add ski goggles and a balaclava to protect sensitive facial skin.

Consider a quick warm up and stretch session for a safer shoveling session. Get your blood pumping with some light activity like jumping jacks, walking in place or climbing up and down the stairs in your home. Gently stretch major muscle groups before heading outside.

Recent findings suggest that snow shovels are not all created equal. For safer shoveling, choose one that is less demanding on your back, joints and heart. Ergonomic shovels feature a curved handle that reduces back strain when lifting. Snow plow shovels are meant to push snow only, not lift it. And battery-powered shovels act like mini-snowblowers to rapidly remove snow without any manual input.

Keep your back straight, bend at the knees and use your legs to lift snow for safer shoveling. Keep the loaded shovel close to your body, then, without twisting, turn your body toward the direction you place the snow. If snow is wet or deeper than six inches, remove it in smaller layers, rather than one heavy shovelful.

Sources indicate that “It is often underestimated what kind of physical workload is required to shovel a substantial amount of snow,” Serwer notes. That’s why it’s notable to pace yourself, stop regularly and strategy ahead to avoid overexertion. Opt for a slow and steady pace, especially if you’re typically sedentary. Rigorous snow shoveling will quickly lead to overexertion and cardiac strain. Going slow allows you to focus on safe shoveling technique, preventing possible muscle strains and pulls. Stay well-hydrated when shoveling and take regular breaks to allow your heart rate to return to normal and your muscles to recover.

Stop shoveling if you’re experiencing cardiac distress, cold-related conditions, dehydration or back strain.

Industry observers note that “Shoveling snow can be a very strenuous activity, placing notable strain on the cardiovascular system,” Serwer says. Know the signs of a heart attack before picking up a shovel, like chest pressure, shortness of breath, nausea and radiating arm pain. Stop immediately if you experience these symptoms and seek medical help. “Hire someone else to shovel, especially if you are at a high cardiac risk,” Serwer says.

Dress in layers and cover exposed skin in freezing temperatures and wind. Even with these efforts, frostbite and hypothermia are real risks. Frostbite begins in extremities like fingers and toes, and exposed facial skin. Early signs include pale, cold skin and prickling or numb sensations. Hypothermia happens when core body temperatures drop too low and begins with clumsiness, foggy thinking, fatigue and intense shivering. Stop immediately and go inside to warm up if you experience these symptoms.

It has been revealed that “It is very easy to become dehydrated while working in cold climates,” Serwer notes, as the human body suppresses the thirst response and dry winter air pulls additional moisture from our bodies. Notice signs of dehydration like fatigue, dry throat, cracked lips or a headache. “Dehydration is often overlooked, and people don’t replace the fluids as needed,” Serwer adds. Stop and take regular water breaks and continue drinking fluids for the remainder of the day if you notice these signs.

Shoveling puts strain on your spine and back, and can lead to serious, long term injuries like herniated disks, sciatica and lower back strains if you’re not careful. Beyond always lifting with your legs, stop shoveling if you feel the early signs of spine and back strain. These include a dull, aching in your lower back, sharp pain when bending or twisting, muscle cramping or shooting pains.

It is safer to push snow rather than lift it.

Individuals with heart disease, obesity, diabetes and high blood pressure should not shovel snow. Those over 45 years old should also exercise caution.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Those roadside scales do more than weigh semitrucks. Here’s what inspectors check and what happens when a truck pulls into a weigh station.

Sources indicate that drivers pass truck weigh stations all the time, but few know everything these stations do or what happens when a truck pulls in. Once a semitruck exits and rejoins the highway, it’s hard to tell what goes on in between.

Learn what happens when a truck pulls in, what inspectors look for, and why some drivers can keep going.

Truck weigh stations help states enforce weight limits and spot safety problems. Trucks can weigh too much overall or carry too much weight on certain axles, putting extra strain on roads and bridges. On the Interstate System, the standard federal limits are 80,000 pounds gross vehicle weight, 20,000 pounds on a single axle, and 34,000 pounds on a tandem axle. Federal bridge weight rules and certain exceptions can also affect how much a truck may legally carry. Limits on other roads can vary.

Recent findings suggest that rules vary by state. “Some require all commercial motor vehicles to stop, while others require only those above a certain weight to stop,” according to the Federal Highway Administration. “Ultimately, States must certify that they are enforcing their weight limits on certain highways in order not to jeopardize their receipt of Federal highway funds.”.

Drivers who pull in follow signs directing them to a scale, where their trucks are weighed either while moving slowly or at a complete stop. If the weight is within the limits, they may be cleared to leave. Inspectors may still pull a truck aside for a closer look even when its weight is fine, based on screening results, visible defects, or random selection. An overweight truck may also be inspected further.

In a recent development, inspectors may check a truck’s tires, brakes, lights, and cargo, along with the driver’s records. They may also review credentials and permits, such as registration and fuel-tax paperwork, along with the driver’s hours-of-service logs. “There are eight levels of inspections ranging from the Level I Inspection, which evaluates both the driver and vehicle, to inspection levels with a more specific area of focus, such as Level VI for radioactive materials and Level VIII for electronic inspections,” according to the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance.

Drivers of overweight trucks may receive a citation or have to move or remove some cargo before leaving. The exact consequences vary by state and violation.

Industry observers note that more serious safety problems, like faulty brakes, can put a truck or driver out of service. A truck placed out of service can’t return to the road until the problem is fixed. Drivers placed out of service must wait until their restrictions end.

Some trucks can skip the stop altogether through electronic bypass programs. These programs use safety records and other information to determine whether a driver can continue without entering the station. Drivers still have to follow any signs or signals telling them to stop.

Florida Law Allowing Bar Liability for Knowingly Serving "Habitually Addicted" Doesn't Apply When Server Only Saw One Drinking Session

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Family 5, Inc., decided Wednesday by Florida Court of Appeal Chief Judge Jonathan Gerber, joined by Judges Marlon Weiss and Johnathan Lott:.
  • In this personal injury case, the plaintiff appeals from the circuit court's final summary judgment which found … that the plaintiff could not prove her negligence action against a bar which had served her alcoholic beverages before she was injured later that night.
  • Liability for injury or damage resulting from intoxication.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From Croteau v. Family 5, Inc., decided Wednesday by Florida Court of Appeal Chief Judge Jonathan Gerber, joined by Judges Marlon Weiss and Johnathan Lott:.

In this personal injury case, the plaintiff appeals from the circuit court's final summary judgment which found … that the plaintiff could not prove her negligence action against a bar which had served her alcoholic beverages before she was injured later that night. The summary judgment rested on the circuit court's application of "the dram shop statute"—section 768.125, Florida Statutes (2020):.

Liability for injury or damage resulting from intoxication. A person who sells or furnishes alcoholic beverages to a person of lawful drinking age shall not thereby become liable for injury or damage caused by or resulting from the intoxication of such person, except that a person who willfully and unlawfully sells or furnishes alcoholic beverages to a person who is not of lawful drinking age or who knowingly serves a person habitually addicted to the use of any or all alcoholic beverages may become liable for injury or damage caused by or resulting from the intoxication of such minor or person.

The underlined second exception is at concern here…. In addressing "what constitutes 'knowledge' in order for a vendor's conduct to be found negligent," the [Florida Supreme Court has] found:.

In a recent development, [T]he cause of action [under section 768.125's second exception] only requires evidence that the vendor had knowledge that the individual the vendor served was a habitual drunkard. Serving an individual multiple drinks on one occasion would be insufficient, in and of itself, to establish that the vendor knowingly served a habitual drunkard alcoholic beverages. On the other hand, serving an individual a substantial number of drinks on multiple occasions would be circumstantial evidence to be considered by the jury in determining whether the vendor knew that the person was a habitual drunkard….

[In another case,] we affirmed a summary judgment for the defendant bar, where the plaintiff patron was unknown to the bar's staff, was not a bar regular, and had purchased up to four drinks over two to three hours. We held that we could not impute notice of the patron's alcohol addiction to the bar when the patron had not shown any signs of intoxication, despite his alcohol consumption ….

Here, consistent with [those precedents], the bar's serving the alcoholic beverages to the plaintiff for the first time on the incident date, without more, should not be considered sufficient evidence to impute knowledge to the bar that the plaintiff was "habitually addicted to the use of any or all alcoholic beverages." ….

In a recent development, roster v. Moulton (Fla. App. 1992)—the primary case upon which the plaintiff relies—is distinguishable….

[In Roster,] [i]t is undisputed that [the patron] consumed 8–10, 12–ounce cans of beer and two straight shots of tequila over the period of an hour and a half. After a short absence from [the bar], during which [the patron] drank yet another beer served elsewhere, [the patron] returned to [the bar's] walk-up window, where he ordered and was served another beer. The [bar manager] admitted that it would be unusual for a person to consume that many beers and two shots of tequila without showing signs of intoxication. Despite [the patron's] considerable alcohol consumption, [the patron] did not stagger and did not slur his speech. The manager twice asked [the patron] to leave the bar only because [the patron] became loud and argumentative. [The patron] pled guilty to the charge of driving while under the influence of alcohol and admitted that he had a drinking problem from the age of sixteen, which he still had at the time of the accident. At that time, [the patron] had never received treatment for his alcohol addiction….

Industry observers note that by affidavit in Roster, "two experts[] … essentially stated that the large amount of alcohol that [the patron had] consumed over a relatively short time period, together with the lack of impairment [which the patron had] demonstrated, would have put a reasonable server of alcohol on notice that [the patron] was habitually addicted to alcohol. [The bar] submitted no affidavits to oppose these viewpoints." ….

However, unlike in Roster, as the bar's answer brief submits:.

It has been revealed that … [W]hatever alcohol [the plaintiff] may have consumed at [the bar], she claims she drank over a five-hour period—much longer than the 90 minutes during which the Roster [patron] consumed 10–12 drinks. Furthermore, [the plaintiff] claims she sat, ordered drink(s), and watched television for five hours, which is much different than the Roster [patron,] who left the bar …, drank another alcoholic beverage elsewhere, and then came back to the bar where he was served yet another drink. Also, unlike … in Roster, there is no evidence that [the plaintiff] demonstrated a level of intoxication consistent with someone who had either a high or low tolerance for alcohol. Finally, unlike the [patron] in Roster, [the plaintiff here] did not become loud or argumentative at the [bar]. By her own admission, she was quiet, not boisterous, not loud, not abusive, and she simply kept to herself….

Unlike the Roster patron, the plaintiff here was an anonymous patron, whose behavior during her visit to the bar was, by her own statements, unremarkable.

Judge Lott agreed, but added that he thought Roster was wrongly decided, including in its reliance on expert evidence:.

Section 768.125, Florida Statutes (2020), says that a bar owner is not liable for damage caused by the sale of alcoholic beverages, except that (as relevant here) a person "who knowingly serves a person habitually addicted to the use of any or all alcoholic beverages may become liable." The language does not require expert testimony, and does not ask how the latest version of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) defines pathologies related to alcohol use….

The statutory language asks whether the server has actual knowledge that the person is, as a matter of habit, addicted to alcohol…. You know such a thing when you see it—and it's hard to imagine being able to see it given only a single occasion of indulgence…. [A]nyone can have too many drinks. What separates a "habitual drunkard" [which is how the concurrence elsewhere interprets "habitually addicted"] is that the habitual drunkard feels compelled to do so on account of their addiction, and does so regularly as a matter of habit….

It has been revealed that turning back to Roster—where was the evidence that the defendant actually knew that the plaintiff was habitually addicted to alcohol? The defendant observed the plaintiff drink heavily on one occasion wherein he handled his liquor well, until he didn't. No evidence of "addiction" was presented, much less of a "habit" of it. The expert affidavits about his apparent alcohol tolerance added nothing to that inquiry.

According to recent reports, in sum, Roster passed the buck from the statutory language to expert opinion, and reached the wrong result in turn. In an appropriate case, we should consider whether to recede from it….

Sources indicate that jack R. Reiter and Robert C. Weill (GrayRobinson, P.A.) represent the bar.

November 18, 2026, 12:42 pm CST.

According to recent reports, A judge in Michigan was found guilty Monday of drunk driving after he rear-ended a public transit bus, but a district court judge ruled that prosecutors failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that his blood alcohol level met the state’s threshold for intoxication. (Image from Shutterstock).

A judge in Michigan was found guilty Monday of drunk driving after he rear-ended a public transit bus, but a district court judge ruled that prosecutors failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that his blood alcohol level met the threshold for the state’s original charge of a more serious offense.

Warren 37th District Court Chief Judge John M. Chmura, 63, was found guilty of intoxication while driving his Ford Fusion into a parked bus that was displaying hazard lights March 25. But the court rejected the charge of Chmura driving with an elevated high blood alcohol content of 0.17 or greater, according to coverage on Law360.

Novi 52nd District Court Judge David Law noted that Chmura’s judgment had been affected, but he questioned the blood alcohol concentration at the time of the crash.

“This court may think it knows the answer to whether or not this was a high BAC case,” Law said. “But thinking it knows is not enough. It needs to be proven beyond a reasonable doubt.”.

It has been revealed that A bus driver sitting inside the bus waiting to resume his route was uninjured in the crash. Sterling Heights, Michigan, police officer Jonathan Journeau testified that Chmura smelled of alcohol, slurred his speech and couldn’t maintain his balance.

Chmura’s attorney, David J. Kramer of the David J. Kramer Law Firm, argued that prosecutors could not establish the higher offense because Journeau failed to determine when the judge’s final alcoholic beverage was consumed.

In a recent development, look, I get it. The Grand Theft Auto series is about living out fantasies, providing gamers a sandbox where they can virtually experience the impossible.

According to recent reports, but still… “House repairs complete” is a bridge too far. Ask any DIYer, and they will tell you no house is ever fully repaired. Pretending home improvement work could ever be finished is just not realistic and really took me out of the experience. 3/10.

Overall, the game is cool. But to be honest, I’m not sure what the point is now that the house repairs are complete.

#90095. Has Congress Learned How To Conduct Effective Oversight?

Has Congress Learned How To Conduct Effective Oversight?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, democratic leaders have promised that their new congressional majorities will focus on affordability and accountability.
  • Industry observers note that listening to some talk about their looks, such as in this Ezra Klein interview with incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia, I wonder whether House Democrats have learned that Congress's oversight and investigation authority is not as all-encompassing as some might think.
  • I discuss the legal contours of Congressional oversight and investigatory authority in my latest Civitas Outlook column.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, democratic leaders have promised that their new congressional majorities will focus on affordability and accountability. They have also pledged to engage in extensive oversight and investigation of the Trump Administration, and firms and individuals that have operated within the White House's orbit.

Industry observers note that listening to some talk about their looks, such as in this Ezra Klein interview with incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia, I wonder whether House Democrats have learned that Congress's oversight and investigation authority is not as all-encompassing as some might think. The authority to conduct inquiries for legislative purposes is broad, but it has limits. And during the first Trump Administration, the failure of House Democrats to contend with those limits hampered oversight efforts.

I discuss the legal contours of Congressional oversight and investigatory authority in my latest Civitas Outlook column. In this piece, I explain why Trump v. Mazars is the greater constraint on free-wheeling fishing expeditions than is the Trump immunity decision.

Nothing in the Constitution expressly grants Congress the power to investigate executive branch agencies, let alone the President (or anyone else, for that matter). The authority to conduct oversight is an adjunct to Congress's legislative powers. In the simplest terms, it is often necessary and proper for Congress to secure information and conduct inquiries as it considers legislation and makes appropriation decisions. Or, as the Court explained in Mazars, this "power of inquiry—with process to enforce it—is an essential and appropriate auxiliary to the legislative function." , , ,.

Industry observers note that no justice in Mazars endorsed the then-common view that Congress could demand all information it sought, subject only to the constraints imposed by Executive Privilege. Rather, the justices were unanimous that Congress lacks the power to investigate for investigation's sake, or to conduct oversight for the purpose of public disclosure or inducing prosecution. Congress has no authority to try private citizens in a committee hearing. As the Chief Justice explained in his opinion for the Court, congressional subpoenas are valid only insofar as they are "related to, and in furtherance of, a legitimate task of the Congress." More generally, congressional subpoenas must serve "a valid legislative purpose," and Congress bears the burden of demonstrating this standard is met. Document demands that appear designed more to harass or punish the political opposition than to inform legitimate legislative activity will not be enforced.

It has been revealed that insofar as Congress wishes to investigate the White House or high-ranking officials, its greatest investigatory authority is not the power to inquire for legislative purposes. Rather, it is the power to impeach. In practice, this means some of the greater restraints on Congressional oversight are political, rather than legal.

Industry observers note that while the Court's decision in Mazars focused on the connection between document demands and the legislative process, this is not the only path Congress may take. The Constitution grants Congress the power to enact legislation for various purposes. It also delegates the power to impeach, and these powers are distinct. As Judge Neomi Rao explained when the Mazars case was before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, "investigations of impeachable offenses simply are not, and never have been, within Congress's legislative power." They stand on their own bottom.

It has been revealed that this distinction matters, because if Congress wishes to investigate potentially impeachable offenses, it must be clear that is what it is doing so voters can evaluate its actions accordingly. "Allowing Congress to investigate impeachable officials for suspicions of criminality pursuant to the legislative power has serious consequences for the separation of powers because it allows Congress to escape the responsibility and accountability inherent in impeachment proceedings," Judge Rao warned. This wolf must come as a wolf.

Recent findings suggest that and on Trump v. U.S., I take a different view than some other legal commentators:.

Some commentators fear that the Supreme Court's presidential immunity decision in Trump v. United States will hamper otherwise legitimate congressional inquiries. "Congress cannot act on, and courts cannot examine, the President's actions on subjects within his 'conclusive and preclusive' constitutional authority," the Court declared. While this insulates the President from criminal prosecution for actions within the core of executive authority and would accordingly limit the Congress' ability to subpoena related information for legislative oversight purposes, it is no shield in matters of impeachment.

Aggressive Congressional oversight of the executive branch is not new. Nor is the politicization of oversight. Once political parties emerged, it was inevitable that party loyalty would rival (if not overcome) each branch's institutional imperatives. Oversight fights were once more political than legal, but Congress could also defend its prerogatives without invoking the courts. A Congress that legislates and appropriates through regular order has more weapons to deploy and a greater ability to force executive branch acquiescence. Insofar as the next round of oversight fights are resolved in court, it will be yet another sign of Congress's decline.

For a deeper dive, my Cato Supreme Court Review article on the Mazars and Vance decisions is here.
