    Tech Report: World Court Finds Myanmar Committed Rohingya Genocide

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1182 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (The Hague) – The International Court of Justice’s (ICJ) landmark ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya is a historic milestone in their long quest for justice, Human Rights Watch stated today.
    • Industry observers note that in the case brought by Gambia against Myanmar for alleged violations of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (Genocide Convention), the court ruled for Gambia, with a nine to six vote by the judges, that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya.
    • “The landmark International Court of Justice ruling is long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured from Myanmar’s military,” remarked Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (The Hague) – The International Court of Justice’s (ICJ) landmark ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya is a historic milestone in their long quest for justice, Human Rights Watch stated today. On November 19, 2026, the ICJ found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya during the 2016-2017 “clearance operations,” carried out by Myanmar’s military.

    Industry observers note that in the case brought by Gambia against Myanmar for alleged violations of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (Genocide Convention), the court ruled for Gambia, with a nine to six vote by the judges, that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. This is the first time that the ICJ found a country responsible for committing genocide. The court also found that Myanmar violated other obligations under the Genocide Convention, including the obligations to punish those responsible for genocide and to prevent genocide. The court’s ruling is final and cannot be appealed.

    “The landmark International Court of Justice ruling is long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured from Myanmar’s military,” remarked Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch. “The ruling also provides a significant precedent for victims of genocide and other grave crimes across the world in their own search for justice.”.

    In August 2017, Myanmar’s security forces began a sweeping campaign of massacres, rape, and arson against ethnic Rohingya in northern Rakhine State that forced more than 700,000 people to flee to neighboring Bangladesh. In November 2019, Gambia filed a case before the ICJ alleging that Myanmar’s atrocities against the Rohingya constitute genocide and violate the Genocide Convention. This was also the first time that a country without any direct connection to the alleged crimes used its membership in the Genocide Convention to bring a case before the ICJ.

    The ICJ is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations, adjudicating disputes between states and issuing advisory opinions on international law. It consists of 15 judges elected by the UN General Assembly and Security Council for nine-year terms.

    In its ruling, the ICJ found that the evidence before it established that Myanmar’s security forces, and other state organs, intentionally committed the genocidal acts of killing, causing serious bodily or mental harm, and imposing measures intended to prevent births against the Rohingya.

    Considering the totality of the evidence, the court concluded that Myanmar committed these acts with the requisite genocidal intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population of Myanmar. To reach this conclusion, it considered an array of relevant factors, including the general context, the selective targeting of the Rohingya, acts that violated the foundations of the Rohingya group, such as sexual violence and targeting children, and the systematic nature of Myanmar’s actions.

    In a recent development, based on these factors, the court found that Myanmar’s genocidal intent was “the only reasonable inference” that could be drawn from the evidence before it. The judges rejected the possibility that other alternative intents, such as to carry out counterinsurgency operations or to forcibly displace the Rohingya, could reasonably explain Myanmar’s conduct.

    In light of its findings, the court ordered Myanmar to cease its ongoing violations of the Genocide Convention, including its failure to enact legislation to give effect to the convention and its failure to investigate, prosecute, and punish genocide. It found that Myanmar needs to provide assurances of non-repetition and is obliged to prevent similar violations in the future.

    The court also established that Gambia was entitled to seek reparations on behalf of Rohingya victims and ordered Myanmar to provide them. These include forms of restitution such as allowing and facilitating the safe, voluntary and dignified return of the Rohingya to their place of residence, and the reunification of displaced families. Whenever restitution is materially impossible, the court ordered Myanmar to provide reparations in the form of compensation.

    According to recent reports, the court’s reasoning in this case is expected to have a profound impact on other pending cases before the ICJ regarding alleged violations of the Genocide Convention. This includes the case filed by South Africa against Israel in December 2023.

    It has been revealed that prior to the Myanmar judgment, US officials sought to pressure the ICJ and its judges with regard to the legal threshold for genocide. The US government has already sanctioned the International Criminal Court and several of its officials in an effort to shield senior US and Israeli officials from facing serious crimes charges before the court.

    Industry observers note that in February 2021, following the November 2020 Myanmar elections won by Aung San Suu Kyi’s National League for Democracy, the then-commander-in-chief, Sr. Gen. Min Aung Hlaing, led a military coup that overthrew the civilian government. More than five years later, Myanmar’s military junta continues to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity throughout the country. Min Aung Hlaing installed himself as president through fraudulent elections in December 2025 and January 2026.

    Industry observers note that in Rakhine State since late 2023, Rohingya civilians have been caught in the hostilities between the junta and ethnic Arakan Army forces. Both parties have carried out grave abuses, including extrajudicial killings, widespread arson, and unlawful recruitment. The Myanmar military continues to commit war crimes against the Rohingya and the crimes against humanity of apartheid, persecution, and deprivation of liberty. The Arakan Army, which now controls most of Rakhine State, has tightened repression of the Rohingya, including forced labor and arbitrary detention, and has committed grave violations of the laws of war amounting to war crimes.

    ICJ judgments are legally binding on the parties to the case. If one party considers that the other has failed to comply with the court’s ruling, it may turn to the Security Council, which can “make recommendations or decide upon measures to be taken to give effect to the judgment.” The Security Council has never acted upon this discretionary power.

    The UN General Assembly can galvanize political support to enforce ICJ judgments by adopting resolutions calling for compliance. Individual countries can also influence compliance through their bilateral engagement with the relevant party.

    Eleven countries that are parties to the Genocide Convention intervened in Gambia’s case on limited issues relating to the construction of the convention. The court’s interpretation of the convention on these issues becomes legally binding for them.

    The ICJ ruling is a clear reminder of the importance of independent judicial institutions in upholding international law, Human Rights Watch noted.

    “Myanmar should swiftly comply with the World court’s judgment and end its oppression of the Rohingya,” Vignoli said. “Concerned governments should strongly support the Rohingya and promote justice for atrocities, press Myanmar’s junta to comply with the judgment, and ensure the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar.”.

    Industry News: 2026 Year in Review: When AI dominated the room

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1043 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, I’ve been writing this column for nearly nine years, and over the past year, I’ve seen legal professionals adapt to new technology faster than ever before.
    • Recent findings suggest that at record pace, established legal technology companies have embedded AI into their products, rolled out AI-enabled features, and connected consumer-grade AI to their platforms using model context protocol connectors.
    • Industry observers note that it was a year of rapid change, making it challenging for lawyers to keep up.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, I’ve been writing this column for nearly nine years, and over the past year, I’ve seen legal professionals adapt to new technology faster than ever before. At the same time, technology has advanced exponentially, with artificial intelligence changing how information is obtained and how work gets done.

    Recent findings suggest that at record pace, established legal technology companies have embedded AI into their products, rolled out AI-enabled features, and connected consumer-grade AI to their platforms using model context protocol connectors. Meanwhile, AI startups proliferated across the legal technology landscape, with some disappearing overnight, while others were snapped up and acquired less than a year after launch.

    Industry observers note that it was a year of rapid change, making it challenging for lawyers to keep up. From tracking updated software features and emerging AI-powered technologies to learning how to use AI ethically, lawyers had a lot on their plates. That’s where my 2026 columns came in. Each one offered a summary of the latest legal technology news or provided roadmaps for legal software adoption in law firms.

    According to recent reports, trusts and estates lawyers rely on drafting software to create complex planning documents and manage related estate work. These tools include features like guided interviews, automated forms and shared client information that support document creation and reduce drafting errors. Some software also helps lawyers customize intends and handle tasks such as trust funding and estate administration. Understanding how the options differ can assist lawyers in choosing the software that fits their trusts and estates practice’s workflows.

    Industry observers note that AI systems reflect the assumptions and perspectives of the people who develop them, as well as the data used to train them. Those assumptions can shape AI outputs and reinforce bias, especially when women and other underrepresented groups have little input into how systems are designed. Drawing on the Women + AI Summit, including more perspectives when developing AI matters; it can impact the questions considered, improve outcomes, and determine how these systems affect consumers and the public at large.

    Sources indicate that at Legalweek 2026, agentic AI and the competition to become law firms’ central AI platform were recurring themes. There were also plenty of updates from legal technology providers, from platforms that connected research, drafting and firm data to specialized tools for e-discovery, litigation, legal research and skills training. The conference announcements highlight how companies are building both integrated ecosystems and focused applications that help lawyers incorporate new AI-driven workflows into their firms.

    Industry observers note that drawing on findings from the 8am 2026 Legal Industry Report, this column examines how the profession is responding to rapid AI adoption, access-to-justice hurdles and concerns about the rule of law. The report shows that individual AI use has grown faster than the implementation of firm policies and training, even as survey respondents see technology as one way of bridging the access-to-justice moat. Also notable was that lawyers were most concerned about the rule of law and its continued degradation.

    Industry observers note that the growing number of court filings with fabricated or inaccurate case citations has led to a upcoming category of tools designed to check AI-generated legal documents. Citation checkers can help identify false citations, misquoted language and inaccurate descriptions of case holdings. There are citation-checking tools built into drafting platforms in addition to those found in stand-alone applications, with a focus on their capabilities and costs. Before investing in a new tool, consider whether the time saved through AI research, drafting and citation checking justifies the expense or whether traditional research and drafting may ultimately be more cost-effective.

    As AI takes on routine work traditionally assigned to junior lawyers, it may also reduce opportunities to develop practical legal skills. Training platforms can allow law students and early-career lawyers to build experience through courtroom simulations, interactive exercises and AI- or VR-based practice. These tools allow consumers to rehearse tasks, such as deposition questioning, negotiation and courtroom advocacy, with some offering immediate performance feedback. Using these simulation-based learning platforms, recent law school graduates are better able to bridge the experiential gap and ensure that they have the building blocks needed to thrive in the AI era.

    Partnerships and integrations dominated the news at ILTACON 2026, as legal technology companies worked to connect their AI tools with legal data, software and workflows. In addition to those developments, there were fresh products that streamlined litigation, legal writing and law firm pricing. The conference takeaway was that legal AI is moving beyond stand-alone tools toward connected systems, for better or for worse.

    Litigation teams often work with large, complex collections of digital evidence, which can be difficult to organize and analyze using traditional methods. AI-powered fact analysis tools can assist with the review of case materials by identifying people, events and inconsistencies and by creating timelines that link to supporting documents. These tools can help litigators analyze and understand the evidence and collaborate more efficiently with their teams.

    As newly introduced AI-powered platforms enter the market, solo and small-firm lawyers now have more affordable options for legal research. There are some tools priced at $100 or less per month that lawyers can use to quickly and easily search caselaw and statutes. Some also offer case analysis and citation-checking tools to confirm subsequent case treatment. These platforms provide smaller practices with more options, but lawyers should still weigh the cost and accuracy rates against existing research tools, along with the time required to verify AI-generated results.

    Nicole Black is a Rochester, Latest York-based attorney, author and journalist. She is the principal legal insight strategist at 8am, parent organization of LawPay, MyCase, CasePeer and DocketWise. She is the nationally recognized author of Cloud Computing for Lawyers and is a co-author of Social Media for Lawyers: The Next Frontier, both published by the American Bar Association. She writes regular columns for ABAJournal.com and Above the Law, has authored hundreds of articles for other publications, and she regularly speaks at conferences regarding the intersection of law and emerging technologies.     💡 Key Takeaways
    • The United States has recently made a concerted effort to water down draft resolutions at the United Nations that reference the rights of women and girls, sexual orientation and gender identity, and the International Criminal Court (ICC).
    • The US efforts at the General Assembly’s Third Committee, which focuses on human rights, highlight the Trump administration’s positioning as an outlier among established democracies as it picks and chooses among universal human rights.
    • Unlike in the UN Security Council, where the US and the other four permanent members have a veto and the US has successfully struck out language on the ICC, gender, and other topics — no single country can block General Assembly resolutions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The United States has recently made a concerted effort to water down draft resolutions at the United Nations that reference the rights of women and girls, sexual orientation and gender identity, and the International Criminal Court (ICC).

    The US efforts at the General Assembly’s Third Committee, which focuses on human rights, highlight the Trump administration’s positioning as an outlier among established democracies as it picks and chooses among universal human rights.

    Unlike in the UN Security Council, where the US and the other four permanent members have a veto and the US has successfully struck out language on the ICC, gender, and other topics — no single country can block General Assembly resolutions.

    At the Third Committee, the US targeted language in draft resolutions referencing sexual and reproductive rights for women and girls. For resolutions on violence against women and girls and trafficking in women and girls, the US proposed adding “in accordance with national laws” after such references. The proposed amendments reflect the Trump administration’s efforts to dismantle internationally protected reproductive rights.

    Sources indicate that the US has not been acting alone. Russia proposed deleting an ICC reference from the resolution on trafficking in women and girls. Egypt submitted similar amendments to the resolution on violence against women and girls and sought to remove a reference to “sexual orientation and gender identity” from a resolution on extrajudicial executions.

    UN member countries rejected the amendments and adopted the resolutions.

    The US also voted against a resolution supporting human rights defenders because it included references to gender and reproductive rights. It abstained on human rights resolutions it traditionally supports on North Korea, Myanmar, and Ukrainian territories occupied by Russia because of ICC references. Those resolutions also passed.

    The Trump administration’s assault on the international human rights system has not been limited to UN resolutions. It has imposed sanctions on ICC judges, prosecutors, nongovernmental groups, a UN human rights expert, and the court itself. It has vowed to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick” to prevent investigations of US and Israeli officials.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s heartening that these attempts by the US and others to undermine human rights and international accountability have failed so far. But UN member countries need to work together to resist future efforts to weaken human rights norms and international justice.

    It has been revealed that “Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government,” remarked Attorney General Todd Blanche. “The defendants listed in the indictment allegedly supported two foreign terrorist organizations, and al-Saadi allegedly coordinated with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted terrorist plot. This FBI will use all our resources to detect and stop such terrorist attacks as we’ve done the last 21 months – with over 1,300 terrorists disrupted and nearly 7,000 Foreign Terrorist Organization related arrests, up 1,057%. All those who threaten our homeland will get the message – justice will find you.”.

    “Today marks a major disruption of an alleged global terrorism conspiracy,” stated Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “No matter where they are in the world, the National Security Division of the Department of Justice will pursue those who target American citizens and American interests. My thanks go out to the prosecutors and law enforcement partners for their work on this case.”.

    “As alleged, these defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” stated U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald for the Southern District of New York. “Even after one of their co-conspirators was arrested and placed in federal custody, the defendants allegedly continued coordinating terrorist activity through coded communications and a network of associates overseas. The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real. Our Office will not stop working to address and disrupt this threat, and to prosecute those responsible.”.

Most recently, in approximately September 2026, al-Hassani allegedly orchestrated a terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base (RAF Fairford) in Fairford, United Kingdom (the “RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot”), which at the time of the attempted attack, housed U.S. military aircraft and personnel.

Al-Hassani, who is originally from Iraq, used his contacts and criminal associates to carry out terrorist attacks in the United Kingdom.

    The European Terrorist Attacks were carried out in the name of a purportedly new terrorist group with the pseudonym Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), which is a front for Kata’ib Hizballah and other FTOs. Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the United Kingdom, the most of any European country. The attacks involved arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual U.S.-British citizen.

    According to recent reports, al-Saadi, Mohajeri, and Al-Hassani were allegedly personally involved in planning many of the European Terrorist Attacks, and al-Saadi and Mohajeri helped create and publish online propaganda videos of these attacks. For example, on or about April 6, Mohajeri and al-Hassani planned attacks while together in a room in Iraq with a map of London displayed on a computer screen. In a video of that meeting, al-Hassani told Mohajeri, “we need to get focused on London.”  An image of the video is below, with Mohajeri on the right and al-Hassani on the left. HAYI then claimed responsibility for six terrorist attacks that occurred in and around London starting approximately one week later.

Specifically, al-Saadi, al-Hassani, and Mohajeri, along with others, were in a room watching a FaceTime video with the individual who was carrying out the attack, which was projected onto a large screen against the background of the HAYI logo. Al-Hassani directed the perpetrators’ actions, including by instructing the individual on the other end of the call to execute the attack and directing that individual to take a lighter and “light one in your hand,” “light it,” and “throw the fourth one.” Al-Saadi recorded the attack in real time, while Mohajeri recorded al-Hassani and al-Saadi in the room as they directed the attack. A still image from Mohajeri’s recording, showing al-Saadi (circled in red) and al-Hassani (circled in green), as they directed and filmed the attack, is below.

    Sources indicate that the next day, on or about April 18, al-Hassani participated in another video call with an individual carrying out an attack on a synagogue in London, with the HAYI logo projected on the background of al-Hassani’s screen. During the video call, al-Hassani directed the individual to “light it up like a Christmas tree.” The person on the video then lit an improvised explosive device and threw it at a building. An image from the video is shown below.

    In March and April — overlapping with the time that al-Saadi was co-located in Iraq with Mohajeri and al-Hassani, planning the European Terrorist Attacks — al-Saadi allegedly attempted to coordinate and carry out terrorist attacks in the United States, including by targeting a synagogue in Manhattan.

    On or about May 1, following the European Terrorist Attacks, al-Saadi was arrested abroad and subsequently transferred to the custody of the United States to face prosecution. Al-Saadi has been in federal custody since his arrival in the United States. For approximately four months following al-Saadi’s arrest, there were no additional attacks attributable to al-Saadi, Mohajeri, and al-Hassani.

    In August, however, al-Hassani allegedly directed and paid associates in the United Kingdom to conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot. On Aug. 22, al-Hassani paid one individual (Individual-1) to perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford’s perimeter and al-Hassani subsequently received videos of the area surrounding the base. In later communications with al-Hassani, Individual-1 referred to him as “Ali.”.

    According to recent reports, in September, al-Hassani also tasked and paid several individuals to help him prepare for the plot, including by procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel. At al-Hassani’s urging, those individuals commissioned custom decals that they affixed to the vans to create the appearance that they were used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business.

    On Sept. 26, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base. That day, al-Hassani was in frequent communication with the van drivers, helping to coordinate their movements and directing them where to drive. At least two of the three vans, while en route to the perimeter of RAF Fairford, encountered a security roadblock and were not allowed to proceed on their intended route. Al-Hassani communicated with the drivers and occupants of the vans both before and after encountering the security checkpoint. As alleged, al-Saadi used those calls to pass coded messages to Mohajeri and al-Hassani in the days leading up to the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot.

    For example, in June and July, al-Saadi allegedly spoke with his mother and sister about Mohajeri. During those calls, they referred to Mohajeri by various aliases, including “Abbas, Abu Daniel” and “Sayyid Abbas.”  Al-Saadi also told his family members that he owed money to Mohajeri and directed them to pass along messages to Mohajeri about “work,” a term al-Saadi regularly used to describe terrorist activity, including on social media posts and in discussions with Mohajeri about partnering to conduct terrorist attacks. On one of those calls, al-Saadi also asked his sister, “What are they doing about all our old work?” and asked her whether it had been cancelled or just put on pause. Al-Saadi’s sister responded that “it isn’t cancelled.”.

    On or about Sept. 24, al-Saadi once again spoke with his immediate family by phone. On the call, al-Saadi allegedly inquired about how al-Hassani, whom al-Saadi referred to as “Ali,” was doing. Al-Saadi’s family informed al-Saadi that “Ali” had been transferred to the “International Section.”  Al-Saadi then allegedly instructed his family to “give him [al-Hassani] money so we can do it.”  As described above, three days later, al-Hassani orchestrated the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Sydney) – Australian officials should press the Vietnamese government to release political prisoners and reverse its intensifying repression of human rights during the upcoming 21st Australia-Vietnam Human Rights Dialogue, Human Rights Watch said today. The case of an Australian national Tran Hiep, a democracy and human rights activist, is of particular concern. He has been detained in Vietnam since he was reported missing in Cambodia in September 2026.

    Human Rights Watch urged Australia, in a submission to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, to seek clear, concrete, and measurable progress from Vietnam on issues including political prisoners, labor rights, transnational repression, and freedom of religion and belief.

    It has been revealed that “Since Australia’s last dialogue, Vietnam has sharply intensified human rights abuses both inside and outside the country,” said Daniela Gavshon, Australia director at Human Rights Watch. “Australia needs to make it clear to Vietnam that merely holding another meeting is not itself a measure of progress.”.

    Vietnamese authorities have stepped up transnational repression, reaching beyond the country’s borders to suppress dissent by targeting human rights activists, government critics, and others in violation of their human rights. In late September, the overseas political organization Viet Tan alleged that Vietnamese police had detained three of its members in Cambodia, including Tran Hiep, and transferred them to Vietnam.

    The Vietnamese government currently holds more than 160 political prisoners for exercising their rights to free expression or for peacefully advocating human rights and democracy. Dozens more are detained and awaiting trial. During the first nine months of 2026, Vietnamese courts convicted and sentenced at least 31 activists to lengthy prison terms, including the prominent bloggers Hoang Thi Hong Thai and Huynh Ngoc Tuan. During this period, the police arrested at least 46 other people for criticizing the government.

    It has been revealed that the upcoming dialogue should also focus on Vietnam’s suppression of independent labor organizing. Both Australia and Vietnam are parties to the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, which contains provisions obligating Vietnam to carry out reforms and to allow the creation of independent trade unions. However, as Human Rights Watch recently documented, the Vietnamese government has not actually reformed its policies and practices, and prevents workers from forming and operating genuinely independent unions.

    Industry observers note that the Australian government should communicate concerns about these violations. It should also outline how Vietnam’s failures to reform will affect Australia-Vietnam relations and implementation of trade and tariff provisions in the partnership.

    Sources indicate that “The Australia-Vietnam human rights dialogue will accomplish little so long as concrete outcomes aren’t formalized,” Gavshon noted. “A human rights dialogue shouldn’t be a box-ticking exercise but instead a diplomatic exchange with real-world implications.”.

    Australia revealed on November 18 further targeted sanctions on three individuals and four entities involved in illegal settlement expansion and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the West Bank. Although these sanctions are a welcome step, they are long overdue and don’t go far enough.

    The situation in the West Bank is dire. State-backed settler violence has risen to all-time highs. Tens of thousands of Palestinians have been displaced and 1,394 killed by settlers or soldiers in the West Bank since the start of 2023. The number of illegal Israeli settlements has nearly doubled, including the E1 settlement project, which even Israel’s allies have called a “red line,” and which Israeli ministers openly boast is intended to erase any possibility of a future Palestinian state.

    On the same day as Australia’s announcement, the United Kingdom declared sanctions against eight construction companies and property development firms that have not, until now, been sanctioned by any government. The individuals and companies sanctioned by Australia, however, have previously been sanctioned by the United Kingdom and other states.

    Industry observers note that when the United Kingdom, France, and Canada announced a ban on Israel’s illegal settlements in September, Australia did not join. Instead, at the time, Foreign Minister Wong promised further sanctions to deter illegal settlement, which are the ones just announced.

    Israel’s settlements are illegal. In its 2024 advisory opinion, the International Court of Justice found that all states have an obligation to “take steps to prevent trade or investment relations that assist in the maintenance of the illegal situation created by Israel in the Occupied Palestinian Territory.” Banning trade with illegal settlements isn’t optional. It’s required by international law.

    Australia claims it is genuinely committed to upholding international law while continuing to trade with unlawful settlements that rob Palestinians of their land and livelihoods. Recent reporting suggested that the majority of agricultural shipments coming to Australia marked as “products of Israel” are from illegal settlements.

    It’s past time for Australia to do everything in its power to stop the expansion of settlements, both through a trade ban and targeted sanctions on construction companies engaged in illegal settlement expansion.

    Since early November, many rural communities in the Catatumbo region, near the Colombia-Venezuela border, have suffered violent abuses and forced displacement as the 33rd Front, a dissident group of the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), has clashed with the National Liberation Army (ELN) over control of the territory.

    During a field visit from November 9 to 12, Human Rights Watch interviewed community members, representatives of civil society organizations, humanitarian workers, and local authorities, who noted these groups have continued to kill civilians, recruit children, plant antipersonnel mines, carry out drone attacks, and impose strict social control over communities.

    People told us that on November 8 in Caño Salado, a rural community in Tibú, members of the 33rd Front threatened residents and accused them of collaborating with the ELN. Two community leaders were killed. “They told people to leave, or they would kill anyone who was involved with the ELN,” a civil society member told Human Rights Watch.

    Dozens of families have also been displaced from Bocas de San Miguel and El Diamante, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.

    According to media reports, armed groups have also carried out six attacks using drones armed with explosives in Catatumbo in the first half of November, killing at least five people, including one civilian, and injuring 14 civilians.

    The situation in Catatumbo has been critical since early 2025, when Human Rights Watch documented that armed groups killed, assaulted, kidnapped, disappeared civilians and caused the displacement of more than 100,000 people.

    According to official announcements, since President De la Espriella took office in August, the government has carried out three airstrikes in Catatumbo, resulting in 10 deaths. The strikes were followed by Colombian army ground operations that resulted in six arrests, and the recovery of two children who had been recruited by armed groups. Community members told us these actions have done little to reduce armed groups’ violence and control over communities.

    Industry observers note that the government should urgently protect civilians, by ensuring that its security strategy goes beyond military operations. It should include effective law enforcement and criminal prosecutions, a stronger humanitarian response, support for affected communities, and targeted social and economic policies to reduce the high levels of poverty that fuel the strength of armed groups in the region.

    Recent findings suggest that A recent Newly introduced York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    A recent New York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators.

    The city council passed the ban Thursday, putting an end to a 168-year industry that has attracted a healthy tourist business. Fresh York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani prepares to sunset the carriages by June 1, 2028, in all five boroughs in the city. The union representing carriage operators and owners argues that their livelihood has been taken away and seeks to have the ban struck down.

    “The city’s approach can be summarized in 12 words: immediately cripple the owners, ignore property interests and contracts, and maybe compensate,” according to the suit.

    Additionally, the newly introduced law stipulates the “humane disposition” of the horses. Animal rights activists have in the past expressed concern over the welfare of the horses. Earlier this year, an 18-year-old tourist died after jumping from a runaway carriage—the first fatality since the carriages were introduced into Central Park in New York City.

    “Our city has changed, and now it is time for our laws to change, too,” Mamdani mentioned.

    Bloomberg Law and MSN had coverage.

    Latest Update: No Emotional Distress Damages in Contract Suit Over Placenta

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (640 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, from Staton v.
    • Industry observers note that [Staton] alleges that she contracted with defendant to return her placenta to her after the birth of her son and that Jefferson failed to do so.
    • It has been revealed that in Pennsylvania, it is the general rule that emotional distress damages are not recoverable for breach of contract.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, from Staton v. Jefferson Health-Abington, decided by Judge Harvey Bartle (E.D. Pa.) Oct. 15, but just noted a few days ago in the Westlaw Bulletin:.

    Industry observers note that [Staton] alleges that she contracted with defendant to return her placenta to her after the birth of her son and that Jefferson failed to do so. She relies on a document entitled "Patient Specimen Release Form" which she signed on August 22, 2021. In her prayer for relief, plaintiff seeks the award of "compensatory and consequential damages against [Jefferson] … in an amount to be determined at trial, based on the unique personal, cultural and spiritual value of Ms. Staton's placenta." In addition, she asks the court to "[g]rant such other and further relief as the Court deems just, equitable, and proper." ….

    It has been revealed that in Pennsylvania, it is the general rule that emotional distress damages are not recoverable for breach of contract. The parties have cited no case and this court has found none where the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania has ever held that emotional distress damages are recoverable in a breach of contract action. However, in D'Ambrosio, v. Pennsylvania National Mutual Casualty Insurance Co. (1981) the Court left the door open….:.

    The possibility cannot be ruled out that emotional distress damages may be recoverable on a contract where, for example, "the breach is of such a kind that serious emotional disturbance was a particularly likely result." ….

    [Restatement (Second) of Contracts §] 353, which the Pennsylvania Supreme Court referenced by a different number in D'Ambrosio, precludes emotional damages except in very limited circumstances:.

    Recovery for emotional disturbance will be excluded unless the breach also caused bodily harm or the contract or the breach is of such a kind that serious emotional disturbance was a particularly likely result.

    The Restatement gives examples in Comment a. of cases which fit into the second exception. They are contracts for the proper disposition of a dead body, contracts for the carriage of messages concerning death, and contracts of carriers and innkeepers with passengers and guests….

    Recent findings suggest that in this court's view, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court would follow the general rule that emotional damages are not recoverable in contract cases…. While contracts for the proper disposition of dead bodies allow for distress damages under § 353, plaintiff concedes that she "does not equate a placenta with a decedent's remains.".

    Recent findings suggest that in opposing to the pending motion, plaintiff stresses her allegations that her placenta had personal, cultural, and spiritual value to her and that she suffered emotional distress when it was not returned to her. Even if true, her subjective reaction to the alleged breach of contract is not relevant to the matter before the court. In Pennsylvania, emotional distress damages are generally not recoverable in a breach of contract action. Whether emotional distress damages would ever be recoverable would depend on the type of contract or breach alleged, not on the plaintiff's emotional or mental state.

    It has been revealed that the standard set forth in § 353 is an objective one. No case suggests that the application of § 353 or the allowance of emotional distress damages would be decided based on the effect of the breach on the particular plaintiff without regard to the type of contract or breach involved. Otherwise, the floodgates would be open to emotional distress damages in virtually every breach of contract action….

    The result might in principle have been different in a tort lawsuit for conversion, since emotional distress damages are generally available in such torts; but it's not clear that ejected parts of the body such as the placenta would be treated as property under Pennsylvania law for conversion purposes.

    Joseph Hoynoski and Jeffrey Chomco (Marshall Dennehey, P.C.) represent defendants.

    West Bank: Israeli Authorities Harass, Arrest Activists Protecting Palestinian Farmers

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Beirut) – Israeli authorities are detaining activists and community organizers attempting to protect Palestinian farmers during what the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) has recorded as the most violent West Bank olive harvest season in its 20 years of records, Human Rights Watch remarked today.
    • In a recent development, between October 1 and 26, 2026, OCHA recorded 397 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage, the highest monthly figure it has recorded since its documentation began in 2006.
    • “The olive harvest season should be a period of joy, strengthened community, and income for thousands of Palestinian families, but rising settler violence and harsh restrictions by the Israeli military have turned it into a period of anxiety and fear,” remarked Sarah Sanbar, acting Israel and Palestine director at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Beirut) – Israeli authorities are detaining activists and community organizers attempting to protect Palestinian farmers during what the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) has recorded as the most violent West Bank olive harvest season in its 20 years of records, Human Rights Watch remarked today.

    In a recent development, between October 1 and 26, 2026, OCHA recorded 397 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage, the highest monthly figure it has recorded since its documentation began in 2006. Israeli soldiers were present in 26.5 percent of such incidents documented by the Israeli human rights organization Yesh Din between September 27 and October 14. The Israeli military has detained hundreds of people trying to protect Palestinian farmers during their harvest, according to local media reports.

    “The olive harvest season should be a period of joy, strengthened community, and income for thousands of Palestinian families, but rising settler violence and harsh restrictions by the Israeli military have turned it into a period of anxiety and fear,” remarked Sarah Sanbar, acting Israel and Palestine director at Human Rights Watch. “Rather than stopping settler violence, the Israeli military is detaining the people trying to ensure that Palestinian farmers can safely harvest their olives.”.

    According to recent reports, human Rights Watch interviewed four activists organizing groups or volunteers protecting Palestinians harvesting their olives, two of whom had been detained and released since 2025. Human Rights Watch wrote to the Israeli military on November 16; its responses are reflected below.

    Settler violence in the West Bank has been steadily rising since the current Netanyahu government took office in December 2022. Settlers responsible for attacks operate with the financial, material, and legal backing of the Israeli state. Attacks by armed settlers often occur alongside Israeli army units or with soldiers standing by.

    Recent findings suggest that absent state protection, Palestinian communities and activists have organized to protect themselves using a tactic called protective presence. This is a form of nonviolent activism and human rights monitoring where international, Israeli, and Palestinian volunteers physically accompany vulnerable communities.

    “[Their presence helps] to deter settlers, or have less violent attacks, and speed up the harvest so people do not have to stay for long exposed in the areas,” Rabie Abu Naim, a Palestinian farmer and activist from Al-Mughayyir village, northeast of Ramallah, told Human Rights Watch.

    According to recent reports, however, the international presence is no longer able to deter settler attacks, or the military’s obstruction of the harvest. “I have been doing this for more than ten years,” an organizer said. “What we used to think could protect farmers no longer works. Since 2023, all red lines have been crossed.”.

    Abu Naim described recent attacks by settlers in Al-Mughayyir, including beatings, burning cars, use of tear gas, and stopping cars on the road: “Anyone who takes the road to Abu-Falah on the western side of the village, which is now the only entry to Al-Mughayyir, states their shahada [the Islamic declaration of faith, said as final words before dying]. They are entering an ambush … they either survive or they don’t.”.

    “This year’s olive harvest season is one of the worst that Al-Mughayyir ever knew,” Abu Naim stated. “[Settler attacks] are becoming an hourly thing, not daily.”.

    It has been revealed that abu Naim was arrested in October 2025 and administratively detained for nine months. “I suspect it was because of coordinating [protection during] the olive harvest season,” he stated.

    Al-Mughayyir’s farmers have been steadily losing access to their olive groves. In August 2025, the head of the Israeli military’s Central Command signed an order for the uprooting of olive trees on 300 dunams (30 hectares) of land in Al-Mughayyir, ostensibly for security reasons after a Palestinian reportedly shot and wounded a settler who had trespassed on the village’s land. According to Israeli human rights group Kerem Navot, settlers from the Shiloh area carried out clearing operations on about 620 dunams (62 hectares), more than twice the area covered by the order, then took over parts of the land.

    In a recent development, “This year, there are no [protection] campaigns for Al-Mughayyir, because there are no lands we can access,” Abu Naim said. “This year’s season, we can say that there isn’t a harvest.”.

    The Israeli human rights organization Peace Now reported in October that the Israeli military had signed orders barring Palestinians from entering approximately 88,300 dunams (around 21,800 acres) of land in the West Bank, 30 percent more than in 2025, unless they coordinate with the military in advance. The military barred Israeli citizens from only 6,890 dunams of West Bank land, Peace Now reported.

    In a recent development, the Israeli army routinely designates areas as “closed military zones” to forbid Palestinian farmers and international activists from accessing their lands. Legally, this means the land is entirely closed to Palestinians unless authorized by the military. Those entering their fields without prior coordination are committing a criminal offence under Israeli law and face potential removal or arrest.

    Community organizers remarked, though, that coordinating with the military does not always guarantee their security. “For Area C [i.e. areas under full Israeli security control and civil administration], it is completely forbidden to go, even if we do the necessary coordination,” Abu Naim said. “If we get there with the coordination then settlers come, they provoke, attack, call the army and tell them they’re being attacked, so the army comes and clears the area.”.

    Sources indicate that activists said that the military has claimed certain land is a “closed military zone” without providing documentation, to deter farmers and activists from reaching the olive groves. “They came to us and asked us to leave because we are in a closed military zone,” said Matten Kadish-Berner, an Israeli activist and organizer with Protect the Harvest. “When we asked them to show us the order, they refused, and in the end, they left because they did not have any document.”.

    The Israeli military told Human Rights Watch that the designation of closed military zones is intended to “prevent friction and public order disturbances,” noting that this year, “ahead of the harvest, a dedicated harvest situation room was established for the first time in the Civil Administration.”.

    Israeli authorities routinely intimidate and arrest Palestinians and deport international activists engaged in organizing protection for Palestinian farmers during olive harvest season.

    It has been revealed that on October 27, Israeli soldiers raided Burin village, south of Nablus, and detained about 60 people, said the Sumood Network, a Palestinian grassroots organization. All were released except Ghassan Najjar, a farmer and rights defender who co-founded the Sumood Network.

    The Sumood Network stated that before the season began, security agents from the Shin Bet threatened to detain Najjar if he continued to coordinate protection for the olive harvest in the Nablus area.

    On November 17, an Israeli judge approved a four-month administrative detention order for Najjar, the Sumood Network mentioned. During the judicial review, the Israeli Military Prosecution acknowledged that the administrative detention of Najjar is related to political activities that are unarmed and nonviolent, the Sumood Network said. The Israeli military said Najjar “is suspected of hurling stones at Israeli civilians,” which the Sumood Network disputed.

    Israeli authorities often detain Palestinians on the basis of secret evidence that neither the detainee nor their lawyer can see. Orders last up to six months and can be renewed repeatedly, with no limit. International law allows detention without trial only as an exceptional measure, for imperative security reasons, with impartial judicial review. When it is used routinely, it becomes a tool of punishment and control and therefore arbitrary and unlawful.

    According to the Israeli organization HaMoked, Israel held 3,101 Palestinians in administrative detention as of October.

    In a recent development, on October 21, the military detained about 80 US, Israeli, and British volunteers helping Palestinians harvest olives near Bethlehem, including now US Congressman-elect Brad Lander, several rabbis, and Israel’s former deputy attorney general. A few days earlier, Israeli settlers attacked a delegation of French, Belgian, and Polish diplomats, Catholic clergymen, and a French mayor.

    Israeli authorities should release all those held unlawfully under administrative detention, end the systematic use of administrative detention, and ensure Palestinian farmers can safely reach their land.

    Other countries should act to prevent further atrocities across the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including by imposing targeted sanctions on those implicated in ongoing grave abuses, suspending arms transfers to Israel, banning trade with illegal settlements, considering suspending preferential trade agreements with Israel, and supporting the International Criminal Court and its ongoing investigations, including by executing its arrest warrants.

    It has been revealed that “Organizing an olive harvest is not a crime,” Sanbar stated. “Israeli authorities should end their repression of activists and instead fulfill their obligations to protect the Palestinian population.”.

    November 23, 2026: This news release has been updated to clarify which activists were released following the October 27 raid in Burin village.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The French Senate on November 20 approved a controversial bill that risks deepening impunity for use of lethal force by police.

    The bill introduces a legal presumption of self-defense for law enforcement officers using firearms during the exercise of their duties, unless victims or their families can establish the use of lethal force was unlawful.

    It has been revealed that because victims’ families lack access to key evidence to assess the legality of police-caused death, placing the burden of proof on them is likely to deepen impunity and seriously jeopardize pathways for accountability where lethal force was unlawful, unnecessary, or disproportionate. This is inconsistent with France’s human rights obligations with respect to protecting the right to life and use of force by law enforcement.

    In a recent development, the use of lethal force by police is a major concern in France. In 2023, a police officer fatally shot 17-year-old Nahel M., a racialized boy, during a traffic stop, triggering widespread scrutiny of police use of firearms.

    France’s national human rights body and the previous mandate holder of the independent ombudsperson as well as a United Nations rights expert raised serious rights concerns about the bill, while rights groups, activists, and legal professionals staged protests and petitioned parliament to stop the bill.

    Industry observers note that the Senate’s vote followed approval of the bill by France’s National Assembly on July 7. Unless government officials or parliamentarians refer the bill for constitutional review, the president has 15 days to sign it into law.

    Since 2017, when lawmakers broadened the scope of permissible use of firearms by police well beyond international human rights standards requiring necessity and proportionality, numbers of fatal police vehicle stops in France have risen fivefold compared to before.

    A state cannot delegate its legal duty to investigate to those affected by lethal police force. This reversed burden of proof contravenes international human rights law, which requires states to thoroughly investigate every circumstance of lethal police force.

    Recent findings suggest that if the French authorities are serious about avoiding incidents of excessive use of lethal force, and rebuilding public confidence in policing, lawmakers should drop this bill. The government and parliament should instead focus legislative efforts on strengthening accountability and ensuring that police powers are subject to effective procedural safeguards to protect people from police abuse, discrimination, violence, and, increasingly, disproportionate use of firearms.

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1128 w)

    Journal of Free Speech Law: "An Unsettling Agreement: Meta, Jawboning, and the First Amendment," by Evelyn Douek

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1128 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that the settlement agreement that Meta reached with state Attorneys General in August 2026 is constitutionally unsound.
    • It has been revealed that because these changes are being done under government pressure, the agreement violates the rule against jawboning; Meta's customers should therefore be able to bring a First Amendment challenge seeking to enjoin government actors from enforcing the agreement's speech-restrictive terms, or seeking to have a court declare that those terms are unenforceable.
    • Recent findings suggest that according to the settlement agreement that Meta reached with 52 Attorneys General in August 2026, it is the parties' belief that "the public interest is best served when platforms and regulators work as partners." This may well be true in some, or perhaps even many, cases.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The article is here; the Abstract:.

    It has been revealed that the settlement agreement that Meta reached with state Attorneys General in August 2026 is constitutionally unsound. The changes that the AGs pressured Meta to make to its platforms as part of the settlement burden the rights of third parties—Meta's people—in various ways (some content-neutral, some content-based, and some even viewpoint-based), and yet these terms have so far escaped First Amendment scrutiny.

    It has been revealed that because these changes are being done under government pressure, the agreement violates the rule against jawboning; Meta's customers should therefore be able to bring a First Amendment challenge seeking to enjoin government actors from enforcing the agreement's speech-restrictive terms, or seeking to have a court declare that those terms are unenforceable. Settlement agreements should not be allowed to become a loophole in the First Amendment's protections.

    Recent findings suggest that according to the settlement agreement that Meta reached with 52 Attorneys General in August 2026, it is the parties' belief that "the public interest is best served when platforms and regulators work as partners." This may well be true in some, or perhaps even many, cases. But the settlement creates a system of pervasive and invasive speech regulation, and in that context such cooperation might be said to be "startling and dangerous.".

    Sources indicate that first Amendment doctrine stands for the idea that we should generally be suspicious of government power over speech, and specifically ensures that government actors cannot pressure, or partner with, private actors to "do indirectly what [they are] barred from doing directly." That is: the government cannot evade constitutional constraints by enlisting private actors to impose its favored speech rules on its behalf. A settlement agreement is not a First Amendment-free zone, and the terms of Meta's deal with the Attorneys General at the very least need to be subjected to First Amendment scrutiny. This Article argues that because the Settlement Agreement attempts to evade such scrutiny, it is constitutionally unsound.

    To make the stakes of this argument clear, imagine an alternate settlement agreement in which Meta, instead of promising changes like age assurance measures and time limits on kids' usage of its platforms, agreed to prohibit all users from seeing political content or (to make the point even more acute) all pro-Democrat content. The dangers of allowing such an agreement to escape constitutional scrutiny seem obvious. But because concern about kids' use of social media is bipartisan—and no doubt in part because kids themselves are often excluded from conversations about their rights—the constitutional infirmities of the Settlement Agreement have generally flown under the radar. But kids have speech rights too, as do the adult users of Meta's platforms who will also be affected by this Agreement, and politicians and platforms cannot constitutionally agree to forgo those rights on others' behalf.

    I will argue that the third parties whose speech rights are burdened by the Settlement Agreement can bring a First Amendment challenge seeking to enjoin government actors from enforcing the Agreement's speech-restrictive terms, or seeking to have a court declare that those terms are unenforceable. This is true for settlement agreements that create such burdens on third-party rights in general, because any other conclusion would allow settlement agreements to become a loophole officials could use to regulate speech without facing constitutional scrutiny. And, as applied to this Settlement Agreement in particular, a large number of its provisions may well fail to survive constitutional scrutiny. Many of the content-neutral requirements in the Agreement mirror mandates that states have attempted to impose through legislation in recent years, and while these laws are still working their way through the courts and the case outcomes are mixed, the majority of decisions have enjoined similar requirements as violating the First Amendment. There are also content- and viewpoint-based requirements in the Agreement that are aimed at influencing what kids see online that would almost certainly fail First Amendment scrutiny if enacted as law.

    It has been revealed that considering the Settlement Agreement against this backdrop throws into sharp relief exactly why the First Amendment has rules to ensure that the government cannot avoid constitutional scrutiny by regulating speech through means other than legislation. This fact may be deeply frustrating to some. We are now around a decade into the "techlash" against social media platforms. Despite all these years of concern and debate, the law and politics of platform regulation have made legislative solutions elusive. Attempts to reimagine First Amendment doctrine to give states more leeway to regulate the internet have failed.

    Recent findings suggest that there might be a temptation, therefore, to think of the Agreement as an overdue reckoning that cleverly overcomes these obstacles and finally brings Major Tech's worst offender to heel. Indeed, it may only be the start of the reckoning: A month after Meta agreed to settle, TikTok entered into a settlement with Alabama that is clearly modeled on the Meta Settlement Agreement. States are bringing lawsuits against artificial intelligence companies using the same theories as in the Meta case that led to the Settlement. States may think they have found a new way of achieving their regulatory objectives that does not require passing any laws at all.

    But the First Amendment does not permit the government to evade review by simply changing the instrument of regulation. Otherwise, its protections would be paper-thin. And as frustrating as the government may find the commands of the First Amendment, they are a feature and not a bug of the American constitutional system. It is imperative that courts make clear that settlement agreements are not one neat trick to evade these constraints, lest states conclude they can abandon the hard and vital work of building political will and legislative capacity for more comprehensive legal solutions, and instead regulate through one constitutionally infirm settlement at a time.

    Industry observers note that this Article proceeds as follows. Part I demonstrates how the Settlement Agreement creates burdens on the speech rights of third parties: namely, Meta's users. Part II, the crux of the Article, argues that given these burdens, the Settlement Agreement violates the broad rule against what is known as jawboning—governmental pressure on private actors to restrict the speech of others. Part III takes a step back from the doctrinal landscape and considers what the Settlement Agreement suggests about the reduced ambitions and disappointments of debates about platform regulation.

    How to effectively regulate new and fast-changing technologies continues to be one of the most pressing challenges of our time. Our regulatory solutions must respect the rights of society at large and not merely reflect the interests of the tech companies and the politicians that regulate them. The First Amendment is one essential safeguard in ensuring this is the case.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that azerbaijan’s parliament on November 18 approved sweeping amendments to legislation governing nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) that would expand government powers to suspend and dissolve independent groups, impose new registration requirements, and further restrict their operations. The following day, a court sentenced prominent rights defender Bashir Suleymanli to seven and a half years in prison, the latest in a series of harsh sentences against civil society activists prosecuted over foreign funding.

    The proposed legislation would allow authorities, rather than courts, to suspend NGOs for up to a year for broadly defined violations, including failure to meet transparency and anti-money laundering requirements. It would also expand grounds for court-ordered dissolution to include activities deemed a threat to the “legally protected interests of the state and society”—vague standards open to abuse.

    In a recent development, existing NGOs would have just 30 days after the law takes effect to revise their charters and apply for re-registration. The minimum capital to establish a nonprofit foundation, a type of nongovernmental organization, would increase tenfold, from 10,000 to 100,000 manats (approx. US$ 59,000). Together, these requirements would create additional barriers to establishing and maintaining independent civil society organizations in Azerbaijan.

    Sources indicate that human Rights Watch has documented how existing restrictions on registration and foreign funding have forced many independent groups to close or severely curtail their activities. The European Court of Human Rights has repeatedly found violations of freedom of association in cases involving Azerbaijani civil society organizations.

    Authorities took another strike at civil society on November 19 when the Baku Grave Crimes Court convicted Suleymanli, director of the Institute for Citizens’ Rights, of apparent politically motivated charges of money laundering and abuse of office. Arrested in March 2025, authorities prosecuted Suleymanli as part of a reopened investigation into foreign-funded NGO work.

    Courts have also handed down lengthy prison sentences to other activists prosecuted in connection with the same investigation, including eight years for Asaf Ahmadov and seven years and three months for Zamin Zaki (Zakiyev). Election monitor Anar Mammadli received a 13-year sentence in September following an unfair trial.

    Azerbaijani authorities should withdraw the proposed amendments, release Suleymanli and other civil society activists imprisoned for their legitimate work, and end the misuse of criminal law against independent groups. Azerbaijan’s international partners should press the government to uphold its obligations to protect freedom of association.

    COP31 Failed Climate-Displaced Communities

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (421 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, leaving the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, I can’t shake the disconnect between the reality of entire communities losing their homes to rising seas and some governments’ apathy and obstruction of the process.
    • It has been revealed that I am still in awe of Francis, a community leader from Solomon Islands who traveled to Antalya to share his story.
    • Industry observers note that COP31’s inability to reach an overarching agreement leaves communities like Walande—and hundreds of other communities that have been forced to relocate—to face consequences of the climate crisis on their own.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, leaving the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, I can’t shake the disconnect between the reality of entire communities losing their homes to rising seas and some governments’ apathy and obstruction of the process. The conference ended without consensus on the proposed Antalya Pact—the overarching political agreement for the COP31 climate summit.

    It has been revealed that I am still in awe of Francis, a community leader from Solomon Islands who traveled to Antalya to share his story. “Walande… the birthplace written in my passport, no longer exists,” he told a hushed room. “It is submerged beneath the waves.” His words moved the high-level event’s moderator to tears.

    Industry observers note that COP31’s inability to reach an overarching agreement leaves communities like Walande—and hundreds of other communities that have been forced to relocate—to face consequences of the climate crisis on their own. Despite coordinated calls from civil society, related outcome decisions do not include explicit discussion of displacement and planned relocation, and governments failed to increase funding to help frontline communities adapt. Nor was there recognition of the International Court of Justice’s landmark opinion affirming that governments have human rights obligations to address the climate crisis.

    Recent findings suggest that I leave Antalya holding both heartbreak and hope: the summit remains a vital space for global solidarity. Alongside partners in the Coalition on Dignified Climate Relocation, we brought frontline leaders, policymakers, and funders together to exchange lessons, and push for rights-respecting national policies and increased funding for communities forced to relocate. After watching our immersive documentary Solwata, several government officials and climate fund directors stepped up, committing to support finance and policies for relocating communities.

    Official negotiations fell woefully short, and the UN policy process failed to meet the moment in Antalya. But Marshall Islands, Bangladesh, Fiji, Nepal and other forward-thinking governments are proving that another path is possible. Dignified, rights-respecting solutions already exist—and they can be scaled up.

    Ethiopia, as host of COP32, should learn lessons from Australia and Türkiye’s failures, and center efforts to advance finance for adaptation and loss damage which are vital to protect the rights of climate displaced communities.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that lawyer Steven Cozzi, 41, who worked for Blanchard Law, a small law firm in Largo, Florida, went missing in 2023. Dr. Tomasz Kosowski of Florida was convicted of killing Cozzi and sentenced to death Friday. (Photo courtesy of the Largo Police Department).

    A Florida judge has sentenced a prominent plastic surgeon to death for the murder of a “beloved” lawyer who went missing in 2023, saying the doctor committed the crime in a “cold, calculated and premeditated manner.”.

    Pinellas County Circuit Judge Joseph A. Bulone handed down the death sentence Friday to Dr. Tomasz Kosowski of Florida, who was convicted in September of murdering attorney Steven Cozzi, 41, whom he faced in a contentious lawsuit, Law360 reports.

    Prosecutors remarked Cozzi was last seen entering the restroom of his law office in Largo, Florida, in March 2023. Surveillance video allegedly captured Kosowski walking into the law office’s main entrance on the morning that Cozzi went missing, showing the surgeon carrying a backpack and a large box. About two hours later, the video indicates him walking out of the building with a different clothes and pulling a large cart covered with a red blanket.

    Cozzi, described as a “beloved” person, worked for Blanchard Law, a small law firm specializing in business litigation, bankruptcies and contract disputes. At the time of his disappearance, Cozzi was representing a defendant being sued by Kosowski over medical billing disputes. His body was never found.
